### What Is the Best Type of Metal Roof Underlayment?

Metal roofing systems are more complicated than many people realize. A metal roof is much more than just sheets of metal — your metal roof underlayment will play an essential role in keeping your roof dry and secure. In fact, making sure you choose the right type of underlayment for your metal roof is essential to its protection and longevity.

If you’re looking for the best metal roof underlayment for your home or commercial property, you’ve come to the right place. As your local roofing partner, PITCH Roofing is here to demystify all things roofing. Today, that means explaining everything you need to know about underlayments for metal roofs in Florida!
Why Do Metal Roofs Need Underlayments?


Traditionally, metal roof underlayments exist to protect against water damage in roofing systems that could otherwise be vulnerable. For example, they do essential work for tile roofs in keeping out water that is forced under the tiles by wind-driven rain. So why are they necessary for metal roofs?

While metal roofing sheets do a great job at keeping out rain, even during major storms, that isn’t the only way for water to penetrate your roofing system. For example, condensation can form on the inside of your metal panels, which would damage your roof decking without the proper underlayment.

Not all metal roof underlayments are created equal, though. In fact, which underlayment material you choose for your metal roof will have far-reaching effects on your roof’s performance across its lifetime. With that in mind, let’s talk about your different material options and how they perform!
The Best Types of Metal Roof Underlayments for Florida Roofs
Each climate has its own unique concerns, and that is especially true for metal roofs. Florida’s heat and humidity make a resilient, hardy metal roof underlayment essential for your roof’s protection. And when it comes to your underlayment material options, a few options stand head and shoulders above the rest.
Peel and Stick Underlayment
Peel and stick has many different names: self-adhering underlayment, ice and water barrier, etc. Regardless of what you call it, it’s all the same great protection. This metal roof underlayment is made of rubberized asphalt and self-adheres to create a watertight seal over your roof decking. Additionally, the flexible asphalt is capable of repelling water without cracking or buckling under the pressure.

Since these underlyaments stick easily to your roof, you can also expect a faster roof installation. This is not only convenient, but it helps keep your labor costs down. That’s important, because peel and stick is an expensive option for a metal roof underlayment. In fact, it comes with the highest material costs of your underlayment options: between $0.55 and $0.65 per square foot.

Even with these high material costs, though, many homeowners agree that this underlayment is worth the investment. As the only waterproof metal roof underlayment on the market, there is a lot to love about this material option!
Synthetic Underlayment
Unlike peel and stick, a synthetic underlayment is not rubberized. Instead, it’s made of either polyethylene or polypropylene, two types of synthetic plastic fibers. This is a relatively new roofing technology, but it’s already making waves across the roofing industry.

Because it’s made of plastic fibers, synthetic underlayment is highly resistant to tearing. As an added bonus, this metal roof underlayment does a great job of withstanding high temperatures, which means you don’t have to worry about your underlayment breaking down under the hot Florida sun.

While a synthetic roof underlayment is not 100% waterproof like peel and stick, it certainly comes very close. The plastic fibers naturally repel water, which keeps the water away from your decking until the vents in your roof have a chance to dissipate the water under your metal panels. And at a reasonable cost of $0.25 to $0.55 per square foot, this is a great, budget-friendly roofing option.
Why You Shouldn’t Use Felt Underlayment for a Metal Roof


If you’re familiar with common roof underlayment options, you may have noticed that there has been one important option missing from our list so far: felt. If you’ve ever had an asphalt shingle roof, you likely had a felt underlayment that held up well. But when looking for a metal roof underlayment, felt is one of the worst options you can pick.

This isn’t due to a problem with felt underlayments, but is instead caused by a normal function of metal roofs. As it gets hotter or colder, your metal roof will naturally expand and contract. As the metal sheets of your roof move, they will tear a felt underlayment to pieces. Then the next time water gets under your roof, your protection will already be severely damaged and incapable of keeping the water out.

So even though felt is technically the cheapest underlayment option on the market, we strongly discourage homeowners from choosing this option for a metal roof. With so many better options available to you, it’s best to leave felt underlayments to the shingle roofs!

At the end of the day, both synthetic and peel and stick underlayments are great, hardy options. And no matter which ones you want as your metal roof underlayment, the professionals at PITCH Roofing will be able to help. ### Average Cost to Replace a Tile Roof Underlayment

We Floridians love our tile roofs, and there are a lot of reasons to do so. Not only do these roofs look great on a wide variety of homes, but they offer 50 to 100+ years of protection. Unfortunately, though, your roof underlayment won’t last quite as long. But how much does it cost to replace tile roof underlayment, anyway?

We’re PITCH Roofing, and as your local tile roofing partners, we’re here to talk about this under-discussed piece of tile roof maintenance. Let’s talk about why you need to replace your tile roof’s underlayment and how much it will cost you!
Why Do You Need to Replace Tile Roof Underlayments?
Many homeowners are surprised to learn that their tile roof’s underlayment will need periodic replacing. After all, a big selling point for tile roofs is their longevity! So why do you need to regularly replace the underlayment on a roof that can last for up to a century?

Clay tiles may last for a century, but your underlayment is a very different material. When properly installed, your tiles will sit on battens, small strips of wood that themselves rest on top of your water-resistant underlayment. Your tiles move water off your roof to prevent it reaching your underlayment, but this is not a perfect system. Especially during a storm with high winds, wind can force water under your shingles and into your underlayment.

This isn’t a bad thing — it’s what your water-resistant underlayment is for, after all. Without your underlayment, your wooden roof decking could suffer severe water damage. This wear and tear does take a toll, though. Over time, the water breaks down the fibers in your underlayment, which is why it needs replacing.

On average, tile roof underlayments last 15-25 years in Florida. This means that you will almost certainly need to replace your underlayment at least once in your roof’s lifetime, if not multiple times. Now that we’ve covered the basics of your underlayment and how it works, let’s discuss the cost to replace a tile roof underlayment.
Average Cost to Replace a Tile Roof Underlayment in Florida


When considering the cost to replace a tile roof underlayment, many homeowners worry that they’re effectively going to have to pay for a roof replacement. But the good news is that replacing tile roof underlayments is much cheaper than replacing a roof. How much it costs will depend on a few factors, though.
Tile Roof Underlayment Material Costs
For one thing, underlayments come in different materials, each with its own cost. Prices can always vary, but generally your underlayment material costs will look something like this:

 	Felt underlayment: This is the most budget-friendly option at $0.20 to $0.60 per square foot.
 	Synthetic underlayment: The most popular option, this costs $0.30 to $0.70 per square foot.
 	Rubberized underlayment: Great for warm climates like Florida, this underlayment costs $0.30 to $0.80 per square foot.

As you can see, the material cost to replace a tile roof underlayment is generally low. However, labor will make up a substantial portion of your underlayment replacement costs. Because while this job is much cheaper than a roof replacement, it’s still a lot of work.
Labor Costs of Replacing a Tile Roof Underlayment
A lot of time and labor goes into replacing your tile roof underlayment. Your tiles and battens need to be removed so that workers can access and replace your underlayment. Then your tiles need to be securely re-installed perfectly to ensure that your roof is safe and protected going forward.

The good news is that since you’re not paying for new roofing tiles, your overall costs are much lower than a tile roof replacement, despite the work of tearing off and replacing your roof being similar. On average, replacing a tile roof underlayment costs $1,700 to $4,000 in Florida. In some cases, though, that number can be as high as $8,000.

We never recommend choosing sub-par workers to keep your labor costs down. But choosing local roofers is a great way to lower labor costs without sacrificing quality or workmanship. Because we’re locally owned and operated, we don’t have the same overhead costs as roofing companies with offices across the country. This means better, personalized service at a much more affordable price point!

FAQs About Replacing Tile Roof Underlayments


1. Q: How can I keep down tile roof underlayment replacement costs?

A: There are a few things you can do to keep down the costs to replace a tile roof underlayment. These include using an affordable underlayment material, choosing licensed local roofers, and keeping your yard clear of debris to ensure that roofers have quick, easy access to your roof.

2. Q: If my roof is leaking, does that mean I need a new underlayment?

A: Sometimes a roof leak can be caused by damage to your underlayment. In other situations, though, there could be an issue with one of your roof’s penetrations. If you’re unsure whether or not you need a new underlayment, it’s a good idea to call in a professional to conduct a roof inspection.

3. Q: How can I make my underlayment last longer?

A: If your underlayment is damaged, then there is no way to undo that damage without replacing the underlayment. However, if your underlayment is still in good shape, then you have options. The best way to get more life out of your underlayment is to keep your tiles in good condition and keep up with regular roof inspections. Damaged tiles lead to damaged underlayment, so it’s best to keep your roofing system in top shape!

4. Q: Why don’t shingle roofs need underlayment replacements?

A: The truth is that most shingle roofs don’t last long enough to need underlayment replacements. By the time a shingle roof’s underlayment needs replacing, so do the shingles. Since tile roofs last for so much longer, however, this maintenance becomes necessary to prevent leaks and other roofing issues.

5. Q: Will getting a new underlayment improve my roof’s insulation?

A: Yes, a new underlayment can improve your roof’s insulation, especially if your current underlayment is heavily damaged. Felt underlayment is especially thick and heavy, which can provide additional insulation.

### When to Replace a Tile Roof in Florida

Florida has been loving the tile roof lifestyle for centuries. But even great roofs need replacing eventually. As a homeowner, though, it can be hard to tell when to replace a tile roof. That’s why we’ve put together this handy guide!

PITCH Roofing is your local roofing partner, and that means sharing our expertise with you and helping you take care of your roof. If it’s time to replace your tile roof, it’s best to get the ball rolling before the next hurricane comes rolling our way. To make sure you’re prepared, let’s talk about the common signs you need to replace your tile roof!
Signs It’s Time to Replace a Tile Roof


Every tile roof is different. For example, tiles come in different materials, which affects how your roof will age. That’s why we’re going to keep the various types of tile roofs in mind as we help you decide when to replace a tile roof. Keep reading for our list of essential warning signs!
1. Roof Leaks
If you’re trying to decide when to replace a tile roof, a leaking roof is a common smoking gun. Leaking roofs are a sign that something is seriously wrong with your roofing system. And if you’ve been dealing with a leak for a while or multiple leaks, it’s an even bigger sign that it’s time to replace your tile roof.

When you notice water damage in your home, the damage has already spread. For a leak to happen, the water has to get past your water-resistant underlayment and through your roof decking. This means that the structural integrity of your roof could be in danger. If you act quickly, this can be resolved with a timely tile roof repair. But if your roof displays other signs that it’s time for a roof replacement, then your best bet is to bite the bullet and get a new roof.
2. Cracked or Missing Tiles
It’s rare for missing tiles to indicate when to replace a tile roof thanks to their great wind resistance, but in hurricane-prone Florida, it’s certainly a possibility. More often, though, what we find are cracked or shattered tiles that have received damage in a hail storm or as a result of windborne storm debris.

No matter how the damage happens, the prognosis is the same. If you only have a few missing or damaged tiles, then this is a quick and easy repair. If you have large sections of roof damage though, especially if it’s been left in that state for months, then you may need to start over with a new roof. Broken tiles leave your roof unprotected. And large sections of damage indicate widespread roofing problems!
3. Tile Color Fading
This issue is a more common problem for concrete tiles than clay tiles. That’s because clay tiles retain their natural color, so it’s unlikely to be your sign of when to replace a tile roof. Concrete tiles, on the other hand, are painted a certain color. And over time under that hot Florida sun, UV rays can break down these pigments and bleach your tiles.

Technically, this is not a safety concern and it doesn’t substantially weaken your tiles. However, it does indicate that your tile roof is getting old. For this reason, many tile roofs that need re-painting may also need to be replaced, especially if you’re noticing other issues with your roof!
4. Tiles Losing Their Shape
When your tiles were manufactured, they were fit into a very specific shape. Whether you got barrel tiles, French tiles, or any other style, your tiles were made specifically to help water move easily off your roof. Losing that distinctive shape is a key sign that it’s time to replace your tile roof.

Most tile roofs will never run into this issue. But if your roof has been worn down by Florida’s severe storms over the years, they can start to flatten out or buckle in ways that they didn’t use to. When you notice this issue, it’s a surefire sign that you need to act before the damage spreads to your decking!
5. Tile Roof Reaches Its Maximum Age


Every roof has a maximum number of years it can last. While that number is much higher than average for a tile roof, there is still a limit. But to decide when to replace a tile roof based on lifespan, you’ll have to tailor your numbers to your tile roofing material.

Concrete tiles, for example, rarely last longer than 50 years in Florida. So if your roof gets past 40 years of life and starts displaying issues, then it’s probably time for a roof replacement. While it’s tempting to put off a roof replacement, you won’t be doing yourself any favors if a storm comes and your roof isn’t strong enough to protect your property.

Calculating the maximum age for clay tile roofs is trickier. That’s because clay roofing tiles can last for upwards of 100 years in some cases. However, that doesn’t mean that every clay tile roof will last a century. With these tiles, it’s best to look at both the age and the state of your roof.

If your roof is 70 years old but displays no problems, then it could very well be safe to keep that roof for another decade or two. However, if your clay tile roof is 55 years old and has recurring leaks, then that’s a strong indicator that you need to replace your tile roof ASAP.

### How Much Do Shingle Repairs Cost?

Asphalt shingles are the most popular roofing material in North America, but they’re not perfect. These roofs routinely run into problems over time, especially after an active hurricane season. If you’re like many homeowners, you likely have concerns about figuring out how much shingle repair costs will run you.

We’re PITCH Roofing, and as your local shingle roofing partner, we’re here to give you all the pricing information you need. We’ve got decades of Florida roofing experience under our belts, so while every roof repair is unique, we can give you a good idea of how much it will cost to fix your shingle roof. But first, let’s talk about how your shingles got damaged in the first place!
How Shingle Damage Happens in Florida


There is no shortage of shingle killers in The Sunshine State. With Florida’s hurricane-force winds, humidity, and extreme UV exposure, your shingles have a lot working against them. While your roof will hold out against most of these issues, every now and again, a bit of damage is all but inevitable.

How your shingles get damaged can have a major impact on your shingle repair costs. After all, some issues are much easier to face than others. If you have damaged roof shingles, the damage could be due to:

 	Mold Growth: Nowadays, most architectural shingles come with mold-resistant deposits of zinc or copper to keep your shingle secure. But over time, Florida’s humidity can lead to rampant mold growth. If this spreads, you could need an entire section of your roof’s shingles replaced.
 	Cracking, Curling Shingles: Under the famous Florida summer sun, your shingles need to withstand extreme UV exposure. When they can’t, they’ll start to dry out and curl, leaving your roof without its usual protection.
 	Missing Shingles: High winds can take off shingles during a tropical storm or hurricane. This is especially likely as your roof ages and your shingles become less securely attached.
 	Denting: After a storm, you might notice small dents or “bruises” on your shingles. These are caused by storm debris or hail impacting your shingles at high speeds, and they can threaten the structural integrity of individual shingles.

These are the most common ways that your shingle roof will be damaged. Depending on the cause, you could be looking at very different shingle repair costs. To find out how much your roof repair will cost, let’s look at some general pricing guidelines for shingle roofs!
Average Shingle Repair Costs in Florida


When you have damaged shingles, the solution is often to replace the damaged shingles with new, healthy ones. But depending on the type of damage your shingles have sustained, your roof’s problems could go deeper than just shingle-deep. Let’s see how much shingle repair costs when looking at varying levels of damage!
Minor Shingle Repairs: < $500
Having damaged or missing shingles is usually not a major repair. If you act quickly upon noticing the damage and don’t leave your roof time for the issue to spread, your repair can fall into this lowest shingle repair cost category.

Some signs that your roofing issue will be a low-cost shingle roof repair are:

 	You only have a few missing or damaged shingles
 	The underlayment beneath your shingles hasn’t been torn
 	You haven’t noticed any signs of leaks in your home

All of these signs indicate that you’re dealing with minor, localized shingle damage. If you act quickly, the damage shouldn’t progress and you’ll be able to keep your shingle repair costs low. In many cases, these jobs are best left to handyman roofers who know how to install new shingles and charge minimal rates. For larger, more serious shingle repair jobs though, it’s best to stick with experienced contractors.
Moderate Shingle Repairs $500 to $3,000
This tier of shingle repair costs is more substantial, but it’s still far below the worst-case scenario. This applies to shingle roofs that have substantial damage, but this damage hasn’t yet threatened the structural integrity of your roof.

Signs that you can expect moderate shingle repair costs include:

 	Having a moderately sized section of your roof with damaged or missing shingles (less than 25% of your shingles)
 	Noticing roof leaks in your home, even mild signs
 	Your shingle roof’s flashing has been bent or otherwise damaged
 	Water pooling on the valleys of your roof

For jobs like these, it’s best to choose professional roofing contractors who can help resolve the full scope of the damage. Unlike with minor repairs, these jobs are much more complicated than nailing in a few new shingles. While going with cheaper labor is a potential way to keep shingle repair costs down, we find that homeowners often pay more this way when their issue isn’t fully resolved and keeps causing problems!
Severe Shingle Repairs $3,000 +
When a shingle roof has taken severe damage, the situation requires drastic solutions. These kinds of jobs require a lot of materials and labor, which means you can expect higher shingle repair costs. In the worst scenarios, you may even need a partial or full roof replacement.

If you notice these signs, you might be looking at an expensive shingle roof repair:

 	Having more than 25% of your roof’s shingles missing or damaged
 	Roof sagging
 	Shingle granules in your gutters or downspouts
 	Major leaks or multiple leaks throughout your home

When roofing damage gets this severe, it’s because the problems have spread throughout your roofing system. That means your entire roofing system will need repair work. These kinds of jobs are ideal for experienced, local contractors who know both your type of roof and the local climate.

### Who to Call for a Roof Leak

Being a homeowner comes with plenty of stressors. When your roof starts leaking, those stressors get even worse. You know that leaking roofs need to be repaired quickly before the damage spreads, but do you know who to call for a roof leak?

When you're dealing with a leaking roof, you can call PITCH Roofing to save the day. As veteran Florida roofers, we're experts in fixing roofing problems and giving our customers peace of mind. You don't have to take our word for it, though. Let us show you how we can help with your roof leak!
Who to Call When Your Roof Leaks


Who to call for a roof leak depends largely on the specifics of your roof. In every case, it's best to leave a leaking roof in the hands of experienced professionals. However, which professionals you should call will depend on the specifics of your leak. Every leak is unique, and some jobs are suited to some roofers more than others!
Signs of a Minor Roof Leak
Minor leaks are often best left in the hands of handyman roofers. These are roofing professionals who can handle minor roofing problems like missing shingles. While these roofing professionals are great, they're not ideal for major roofing work. For that, it's best to stick with licensed Florida roofing contractors.

So how do you know if you have a minor leak for a handyman to fix? Here are some of the signs that you've got a minor roof leak:

 	Rusted Nails in Your Attic: Minor roof leaks usually start in the attic. If you notice rusting on nails in your attic, it's a sure sign that water has infiltrated your roofing system. This is one of the earliest signs of a leak, which means that if you find rusted nails, it's the perfect time to call a handyman roofer!
 	Texture Changes in the Ceiling: At the point where you're noticing water dripping from your roof, the leak has already spread a good deal. Before things get to this stage, though, you may notice small bumps or brown spots on your roof. For many homeowners, these are the first signs of roof leaks that they notice.
 	Mold in Your Attic: If you notice patches of mold growing in your attic, there's a good chance you have a roof leak. Mold loves moisture, and if your attic is taking on water from the outside, it's going to get a lot more humid.
 	Peeling Paint on Exterior Walls: Sometimes, water from a roof leak gets into your walls before you notice water coming from your ceiling. If you see paint peeling, especially in a concentrated area, it's a strong indicator that you've got a roof leak.

All of these signs indicate that you've got a roof leak that is still a minor problem for now. This means that you may be best served by a handyman roofer who can patch the problem and get your roof back in working order. When it comes to who to call for a roof leak, though, it's a very different situation for a larger roof leak.
Signs of a Major Roof Leak
When you've got a major roof leak, there is no substitute for experienced roof contractors. Unlike handyman roofers, contractors like those at PITCH are capable of doing any roofing work, including roof replacements. When you're dealing with water damage throughout your roofing system, this is exactly the kind of high-quality workmanship that you want!

When determining who to call for a roof leak, any of the following signs indicate that it's time to call in expert contractors:

 	Water Stains on the Ceiling: If you notice dark stains appearing on your ceiling, then you've got a roof leak. Even if you don't see any water coming from the ceiling, staining means you need to act quickly before the damage spreads to the rest of your roofing system.
 	Water Dripping: If you see water coming from your ceiling, it's time to call in roofing contractors you can trust. Water has to make it through several layers of your roofing system to get inside your home, so definitely take this issue seriously!
 	Roof Sagging: Of all the signs of roof leaks, roof sagging is the most serious. If your roof is weighed down in a certain area, your entire roofing system is at risk. Once you notice roof sagging, call leak repair experts ASAP!
 	Musty Smells in the Home: If you notice a musty scent, especially in a certain section of your home, it could be due to a roof leak. Odor in the home means the leak has progressed quite a bit, so it's important to call in the pros before the issue worsens.

Any of these signs indicate that you should call in professional roofing contractors. But at PITCH, we understand that finding reputable, trustworthy roofers can be hard. To help make things easier for you, let's talk about what PITCH can do for you and how you can know that we're the real deal.

### What Are the Different Types of Roof Tiles?

If you’ve recently started looking into a tile roof replacement, you’re probably surprised by the amount of different types of roof tiles. Tile roofing has been a part of Florida life since the first Spanish colonists arrived, and in that time just about every type of tile roof has come to join the Sunshine State. But which one is right for your home?

That’s what we’re here to help you figure out. We’re PITCH Roofing, your local tile roofing partner. As veteran Florida roofers, we know tiles inside and out. Keep reading for our breakdown of the different types of roof tiles you can choose from in Florida!
Different Types of Tile Roof Materials


Among the different types of roof tiles, the material you pick will have a big impact on the look, longevity, and cost of your new tile roof. Let’s look at your tile roofing material options in Florida and how each one will perform for you!
Concrete Roofing Tiles
Concrete tiles are a modern invention designed to lower tile roof replacement costs. Since concrete is relatively cheap and readily available, this material has much lower manufacturing costs. In fact, concrete roofing tiles can cost as little as $7 per square foot, although the costs may be as high as $19 per square foot.

In terms of performance, these tiles bring the classic protection that homeowners love. With wind resistance up to 150 mph, concrete roofing tiles are more than ready to handle any storm. These tiles are also highly resistant to impact damage, so you won’t have to worry about cracked tiles from storm debris or hail. Thanks to this great protection, concrete roof tiles last about 50 years on average, even in Florida.

Different types of roof tiles have their respective downsides, though. For concrete tiles, that’s UV rays. Over time, the sun can bleach your painted concrete tiles and fade their color. This can easily be resolved by having your tiles re-painted, but it is an expense you’ll want to account for before committing to a concrete tile roof replacement.
Clay Roofing Tiles
Clay tiles are a classic, timeless option. This luxury roofing material offers unbeatable performance across the lifetime of your roof, albeit at a premium cost. In Florida, expect to pay $12 to $21 per square foot for a new clay tile roof. This is a major investment, but are clay roofing tiles worth the up-front cost?

Many homeowners would say yes. Like concrete tiles, clay tiles are capable of withstanding the winds of a major hurricane without budging. They’re also Class A fire resistant and have additional resistance to rot, both of which will help keep your roofing system safe and functional for a long time.

In fact, among all the different types of roof tiles, clay tiles last the longest. 50 years is the average number of years that you can count on your roof lasting, but these roofs have been known to last as long as 100 years with timely repairs and proper maintenance. This makes them, by far, the most long-lasting roofing material on the Florida market!
Metal Roofing Tiles
An exciting new roofing technology is metal roof tiles. Made of stone-coated steel, these tiles bring all the protection of metal with the classic look and curb appeal of tile roofing. Contractors install these tiles by drilling them straight down onto your roof. This makes for simple and quick installation, which is why metal tiles cost $7 to $15 per square foot on average.

Metal roofing tiles also boast great protective features. They can resist winds up to 170 mph, have rust-resistant coatings, and are at a much lower risk for pest infestations than other roofing materials.

There are downsides, though. Because metal roofing tiles are an exposed fastener roofing system, they deal with a lot of wear and tear. This means occasional repairs to your roof fasteners and an average lifespan of 30-50 years. Still, as you look at the different types of roof tiles, metal roofing tiles are a viable option worth considering!
Different Types of Roof Tiles


In addition to the different types of roof tile materials, there are also different styles of tiles that you’ll need to choose from. All of these tiles are capable of keeping your roof safe, but they’ll provide different aesthetics to your roof. For that reason, it’s important to choose carefully and choose tiles that complement your home’s overall look.

The most popular types of roofing tiles include:

 	Barrel Tiles (Mission or Spanish Tiles): Shaped like half-cylinders, these tiles are typically installed in an interlocking pattern, creating a wave-like appearance. They’re popular in Mediterranean, Spanish, and Southwestern-style architecture.
 	Flat Tiles: Sleek, rectangular tiles with a modern aesthetic, often used on contemporary or minimalist designs. They can be clay or concrete and offer excellent water shedding.
 	French Tiles (Marseilles Tiles): These distinctive interlocking clay tiles have prominent ridges for enhanced water drainage. They add unique texture and generate visual interest on your roof.
 	Roman Tiles: Similar to barrel tiles but flatter and with a more uniform curve, these tiles offer a classic yet subtle look.

When picking out your roofing tiles, you’ll also be able to pick unique arrangements and configurations. This can give you a completely unique tile roof! With the tile roofing process, everything starts with collecting roof replacement quotes.

### Pros, Cons, and Costs of Asphalt Shingles

Of all your roofing options in Florida, none is more popular than asphalt shingles. What’s not to love? They’re durable, affordable, and available in every color you could imagine. But as Florida’s hurricane seasons become increasingly active, many homeowners are questioning whether asphalt roofing shingles are still the right choice for them.

We’re PITCH Roofing, and as your local roofing partner, we’re here to answer all of your questions about roofing options. Today, that means giving you the good, the bad, and the ugly about asphalt shingles in Florida. Let’s discuss if this classic roofing material has a future in the Sunshine State!
Asphalt Shingles 101


We’re starting off with a basic introduction to what asphalt shingles are and how they work. In the manufacturing process, they start with a fiberglass baseboard. This is then dipped in hot asphalt to entirely coat the baseboard and give shingles water resistance and enough weight to stay put. Manufacturers then cover the shingle in a layer of stone granules to improve resistance to impact damage and UV rays.

This is how old-school shingles were made. Modern architectural shingles are a little different, though. These new and improved shingles get an extra layer of asphalt coating. While this may not sound like a big difference, it makes the shingle much more water-resistant and able to withstand higher-force winds. It also improves how much shingles help insulate your home.

As you can see, shingles are simple and easy to manufacture. But simple doesn’t always mean bad. To see if asphalt shingles are still a good idea for roof replacements in 2025, let’s look at the good and the bad of this classic roofing material!
Pros and Cons of Asphalt Shingles
No roofing material is entirely good or bad; they usually have good and bad qualities. That said, today we’re looking to see if asphalt shingles are still a competitive option for modern roof replacements. That means we’ll be looking at important factors like longevity, hurricane resistance, and cost!
Pro: Low Roof Replacement Cost
Remember how we said that shingles are quick and easy to make? Well in roofing, quick and easy usually means “affordable.” When you couple their low manufacturing costs with their straightforward installation method of hammering them into place, it’s a recipe for an affordable roof replacement.

Asphalt shingles are, bar none, the most affordable roofing material on the market. High-quality asphalt shingles cost between $5 and $9 per square foot. If your roof is near the average size of 1,700 square feet, that means you’ll likely pay $8,500 to $15,300 for a new asphalt shingle roof in Florida.
Con: Relatively Short Lifespans
Old-school 3-tab asphalt shingles would be lucky to last 15 years. Thankfully, new advancements in roofing technology have made it so that asphalt shingles last 20-25 years in Florida. This is a solid lifespan, but it just can’t compete with other options on the market.

Metal and tile roofs both last longer than asphalt shingles. Even exposed fastener metal roofs, which are the most affordable metal roofing option, last for closer to 30 years before they need replacing. So while asphalt shingles are the lowest-cost roofing material, they’re also the material with the shortest life expectancy.
Pro: Can Withstand Hurricanes
Modern asphalt shingle roofs are more than capable of standing up to hurricanes. Thanks to their thick double coating of asphalt, shingles are highly resistant to soaking through even during major storms. And the extra heft enables them to resist winds up to 120 mph.

This means that even during a major hurricane, your roof will stay in place. While nobody can guarantee that a shingle roof will survive direct contact with a Category 5 hurricane, you will be protected against most hurricanes and tropical storms.
Con: Expect Regular Maintenance


It is very rare for an entire asphalt shingle roof to be destroyed in a hurricane. What is significantly less rare, though, is for asphalt shingles to come flying off during a major storm. As the owner of a shingle roof, you should expect to run into minor roof repairs like this throughout the life of your roof, especially after the first 5 years.

The silver lining is that asphalt shingle roof repairs are usually quick and inexpensive. Replacing a few missing or damaged shingles, for instance, takes only a bit of labor and a handful of new shingles and nails, so it’s a very low-cost repair. However, you’ll need to act quickly when issues arise to prevent them from worsening or spreading. Waiting for roof repairs is a surefire way to end up spending more in the long run!
Pro: Classic Curb Appeal
As a homeowner, you want the value of your home to keep increasing. And an asphalt shingle roof replacement is a great way to achieve just that. Since shingles come in any color you can imagine, you’ll have no problem finding the perfect shingles to compliment your home’s aesthetic.

Architectural shingles offer even more benefits to your curb appeal. That’s because their multi-layered design allows for unique patterning. These patterns create visual depth on your roof, which is why they’re sometimes called dimensional shingles. By adding visual interest to your roof, these shingles go a long way in increasing curb appeal!
Get a Free Asphalt Shingle Roof Replacement Estimate

### Flat Metal Roof Types & Costs

Did you know that Florida has more flat roofs than most of the country? Flat roofing is part of the local lifestyle, and local roofers have worked hard to find the perfect roofing material. While classic options like modified bitumen roofing and single-ply membranes like TPO are the norm, more and more Floridians are choosing to get a flat metal roof to protect their homes and commercial properties.

We should know; we’re Florida’s top roofing professionals! PITCH Roofing is a locally owned and operated roofing company made up of veteran Florida roofers. Today, we’re covering everything you need to know about metal flat roofs and how they perform in our unique Florida climate!
Can You Get a Flat Metal Roof in Florida?


The simple answer is yes, most licensed roofers will be able to install a flat metal roof. Historically, roofers haven’t used metal for flat roofs because the biggest concern for low-slope roofs was keeping standing water out. With new advances in roofing technology, though, metal flat roofs can now easily provide top-quality water resistance.

In fact, flat metal roofs perform similarly to sloped metal roofs. This means you can expect a lifespan of 40 to 70 years, for one thing. And just like more and more Florida homeowners are choosing metal roofs to resist hurricanes, you can count on the same stellar performance from a flat roof made of metal. When installed by experienced professionals, metal roofs don’t go anywhere, even during major hurricanes!

Given all of this, yes, it’s safe to say that you can certainly get a flat metal roof in Florida. But that isn’t the only question you’ll want to ask. More than just looking at if this job can be done, it’s important to determine if getting a metal flat roof is a good idea.
Should You Get a Metal Flat Roof?
In many cases, a flat metal roof is exactly what you need to keep your property safe. While traditional options like modified bitumen and TPO flat roofing perform well, neither of them can compete with metal flat roofs when it comes to longevity.

Metal flat roofs also have advantages over other flat roofing materials. For one thing, they’re much more resistant to puncture damage. This means that when hail or storm debris hits your roof hard, metal will hold up much better than an asphalt or rubber roof.

In many ways, though, a flat metal roof’s performance will vary depending on what type of roof you get. While both options can work well in Florida, it’s important to note the crucial differences. To make sure you’re informed for your metal flat roof replacement, let’s look at the different types of flat metal roofs available to you!
Exposed Fastener
An exposed fastener flat metal roof has the quickest and simplest installation of your metal roofing options. With this method, corrugated sheets of metal roofing are drilled down into your roof. This ensures a watertight barrier and reliable wind protection!

Since these roofs cost little to manufacture and can be installed quickly, they come with the lowest metal roofing costs. However, they also come with some issues. Namely, the exposed fasteners that sit on top of your roofing panels. Since the fasteners are exposed to the elements, they can rust and be worn down over time.

Regular maintenance should ensure that this isn’t a problem and that your roof won’t take in any water. However, this wear and tear takes its toll. For an exposed fastener flat metal roof, you can expect 30-40 years of protection. This is far from a long life by metal roofing standards, but it’s still quite a long life for a flat roof, which makes it a popular option for flat roofs in Florida!
Hidden Fastener
A hidden fastener flat metal roof is more complex than exposed fastener metal roofing, but its complexity comes with advantages. With this metal roofing style, your metal metal panels are mostly flat, with one elevated section where the panels fit together. This is where your fasteners go: underneath the panel, where they’re protected and safe.

Of course, these flat metal roofs are more expensive to manufacture and take longer to install because of their more complex design. Even so, many homeowners find that they’re worth the investment. Since your fasteners are hidden beneath the metal roofing panels, they’re much better protected and age more slowly. That’s why hidden fastener flat metal roofs last for up to 70 years on average!

Hidden fastener metal roofs are sleek and offer top-tier protection. While their price can be off-putting for some, there really is no better option for a long-lasting, durable flat metal roof.
How Much Does a Metal Flat Roof Cost


When it comes to roofing costs, flat metal roofs usually cost more than other flat roofing materials. There is a spectrum for these things, though, and there are certainly ways to make your flat metal roof more affordable. In fact, one of the biggest factors in your roof replacement costs is which type of metal roofing you choose.

Exposed fastener metal roofing costs $7 to $12 per square foot to install, on average. On a 1,700-square-foot flat roof, this puts your roof replacement costs between $11,900 and $20,400. This is expensive for a flat roof, but quite affordable compared to other metal roofing systems!

Standing seam roofs cost $10 to $35 per square foot, which means even a low-cost standing seam roof is expensive. Using that same standard of a 1,700-square-foot roof, you’re looking at costs between $17,000 and $59,500. This is an expensive roof by any metric, but given the quality of the product, many homeowners choose to see the price as an investment in the protection and value of their homes!

### Metal Shingle Roof Cost

Metal shingles offer a lot to Florida homeowners. They have all the strength of metal while retaining the classic, cozy appeal of shingle roofing. But how much does a metal shingle roof cost in Florida?

That’s exactly the question we’re here to answer. We’re PITCH Roofing, and if all you want is the average cost of a metal shingle roof in Florida, that number is $25,550. Metal Shingle Roof Material Costs


The first factor to consider when calculating how much a metal shingle roof costs is the price of your materials. Metal roofing shingles are made from steel roofing sheets that are molded into the shape of shingles and then coated in a layer of stone granules of your chosen color. This is, all things considered, a pretty simple process.

That’s good, because simple manufacturing means lower costs. In Florida, manufacturing costs for metal shingle roofs range from $5 to $11 per square foot. This may not seem especially affordable when compared to asphalt shingles, but in terms of metal roofing, these numbers are quite low.

This is a very wide range, and material costs are certainly not the only pricing factor you need to account for. Let’s help you get a realistic price expectation by looking at the other factors that will determine how much your metal shingle roof costs.
Cost to Install Stone-Coated Steel Roofing Shingles

Other Metal Shingle Roof Cost Factors

However, this range is also quite large. So how do you know if your number will fall at the lower or higher end of this spectrum?

 	Size: Simply put, the bigger your roof, the more expensive it is to replace. Additionally, having many hills and valleys on your roof will increase material and labor costs, since this adds to your square footage and makes installation more difficult.

 	Decking: Your metal shingles will sit on top of wooden roof decking. But if this decking is damaged, it may need replacing. There is no way to know if decking needs replacing without tearing off your old roof, so this can slightly increase your roof replacement costs if large sections of decking need replacing (usually due to water damage).

All of these factors will play a role in your metal roof replacement costs. But the only way to get an accurate price is to sign up for a roofing estimate!

### Residential Steel Roofing in Florida: What You Need to Know

As Floridians try to adjust to increasingly active hurricane seasons, more and more homeowners are turning to residential steel roofing. Steel roofing has grown exponentially in popularity in recent years, but there are still a lot of things you should know about these roofs before committing.

We’re here to dispel the mysteries around metal roofing in Florida. As your local roofing partner, at PITCH Roofing we aren’t just interested in selling you an expensive metal roof. We’re more concerned with making sure you get the best roof for your home at a fair, honest price. Keep reading for everything you need to know about steel roofing for Florida homes!
What Homeowners Should Know About Residential Steel Roofing
Like any roofing style, residential steel roofing has its ups and downs. Its unique roofing factors make it great for some homes, but less than ideal for others. To make sure you know all the essential facts before committing to a metal roof replacement, we’re covering all the essential things you need to know about steel roofing!
Residential Steel Roofing Is Great at Facing Hurricanes


When it comes to holding up against hurricane season, nothing beats residential steel roofing. These roofs are strong, durable, and last for a long time. But what kind of performance can you expect from your new steel roof?

Some of the most pertinent safety features of steel roofing include:

 	Wind resistances between 140 and 180 mph, depending on the type of steel roof
 	40-70 years of longevity and protection
 	Class A fire resistance
 	Rust and corrosion resistance thanks to anti-rust alloys
 	Resistance to damage from UV rays

For all of these reasons, a steel roof is a great investment in protecting your home against hurricanes. While shingles are great, they simply can’t compete with residential steel roofing!
There Are Different Types of Steel Roofing
While many homeowners tend to think of residential steel roofing as one type of roof, there are actually many variations of this style. For one thing, there are two popular types of steel roofing in Florida. Galvanized steel is coated in a protective layer of aluminum, and Galvalume steel has a coating of both aluminum and zinc.

This difference may sound minor, but it has a big impact. For one thing, Galvalume steel is more resistant to rust and corrosion than galvanized steel thanks to its self-healing zinc alloy. On the other hand, Galvalume steel is also more vulnerable to scratches in its protective coating, which makes it a poor choice for roofs that will see a lot of traffic.

There are cost differences to consider as well. Galvanized steel tends to cost $5 to $10 per square foot in materials. Galvalume steel costs a bit more at $6 to $14 per square foot. While we don’t generally recommend basing 100% of your decision on cost, we know that roofing costs are often a deciding factor when planning a metal roof replacement!
You Shouldn’t Install Steel Roofs Near the Coasts
Both galvanized and Galvalume steel make great residential steel roofing materials. But they aren’t well-suited to every environment. In Florida, our coastal areas have a large salt content in the air from the Gulf or Atlantic Ocean, depending on which side of the state you’re on. In either case, this saltwater in the air can greatly speed up rust and corrosion on your steel roof, even with rust-resistant coatings.

You can still have a residential steel roof in Florida. And in most parts of the state, this is a great idea! As long as you are more than one mile away from the coast, your roof shouldn’t be at any increased risk of corrosion. This means that unless you’re directly on the coast, residential steel roofing is still a good idea.

If you do live right on the coast, you still have metal roofing options. We would just recommend that you choose an aluminum metal roof. These roofs are completely impervious to rust, which makes them the perfect choice for coastal Florida homes!
There Are Different Ways to Install a Steel Roof on a Home


Just like there are different types of steel roofing materials, you have options when it comes to installing residential steel roofing. With metal roofing, there are two popular ways to install your new roof: exposed fasteners and hidden fasteners.

With exposed roof fasteners, contractors drill your new steel panels straight down into your roof. This makes sure your roof won’t go anywhere, even during a major storm! At the same time, though, it leaves your fasteners exposed. Over time, the Florida elements can wear away at these fasteners, which will require occasional repairs to keep your roof safe and secure. On the other hand, this is also a much more affordable metal roofing system.

Hidden roof fasteners work very differently. With these, the steel roofing panels connect beneath the panel instead of on top. This keeps your fasteners safe and protected for years to come. At the same time, these roofs are much more expensive because they’re more costly to manufacture and more difficult to install. But if you want the best steel roof possible, hidden fasteners are the way to go!

Average Price of Minor Roof Repairs
Minor roof repairs are just that — minor. They pose minimal immediate threat to your roof, and they don’t take much in the way of time or resources to repair. These kinds of repairs include:

 	Fixing moderate leaks or multiple leaks throughout your roofing system

 	Partial roof replacements, including replacing roof decking

### Flat Roof Leak Repair Services, Costs, and Quotes

Across residential and commercial structures in Florida, flat roofs are a mainstay. Even the best roofs run into problems sometimes, however, and flat roofs are no exception. This leaves many people wondering what to do when the time comes for flat roof leak repair services.

We’re PITCH Roofing, and as Florida roofing veterans, we know how to fix flat roof leaks and get your roof back in top shape. We’re not just here to plug our great roofing services, though. Instead, we want to share everything you need to know about flat roof leak repair in Florida, including how damage happens, how we fix it, and what it can cost. Keep reading for our comprehensive guide to fixing leaks on flat roofs!
How Do Flat Roof Leaks Happen?


If you’ve owned a home in Florida for long, especially through a hurricane season, then you probably know that a lot can happen to roofs down here. But flat roofing issues are unique. While shingle roofs are primarily damaged by hurricane-force winds, flat roofs have a different set of factors working against them.

When dealing with flat roof leak repair, the cause usually comes down to a couple of things. One of the biggest causes of leaks is impact damage. This occurs when hail or storm debris falls onto your roof at high speeds. This can puncture your roof and create an opening for water to get in. While you may not notice the damage immediately, sooner or later it usually leads to leaking.

Another common problem for flat roofs is UV damage. Specifically, with single-ply roofing membranes like TPO, the sun’s rays can weaken the seams of your flat roof over time. While they are heat-welded to ensure they’re water-tight, this protection can degrade as UV rays damage the seam sealant until water enters your roofing system through this new vulnerability.

With flat roofs, water retention is always a large concern. During heavy showers, it can take time for water to drain off your roof. And if there is any weakness in your flat roofing system, this will likely cause leaks. Now that we’ve covered how these leaks happen, though, it’s time to talk about what licensed Florida roofers can do to fix these issues.
Flat Roof Leak Repair Services

More than that, our goal is to diagnose what’s causing your leak and develop a repair plan to resolve the problem at its source. The last thing we want is for our customers to deal with the same problem a few months after we’ve fixed it!

Once you’ve looked over the estimate and chosen us as your roofers, we’ll schedule your job ASAP. ### Are Metal Roofs That Looks Like Tile Good Roofs?

In Florida, tile roofs are a big part of our history and state identity. At the same time, metal roofs offer unbeatable, modern protection against hurricanes, which increase in strength year after year. These two essential facts make a metal roof that looks like tile the best of both worlds for Florida homeowners.

We’re PITCH Roofing, and we know how to get you one of these high-quality roofing systems. Before you start scheduling roof replacement estimates, though, it’s important to make sure that this is the right roofing material for you. Keep reading as we explain everything you need to know about metal tile roofing in Florida!
What Is a Metal Roof That Looks Like Tile?


When homeowners first hear about metal roofing tiles, they often have questions. And it’s right to be curious, because the process of making these tiles is more complicated than many homeowners realize.

This isn’t the only advantage of a metal roof that looks like tile, either. Remember how we said that metal roofing tiles are made in strips? This makes installing them much faster. A faster roof replacement means lower labor costs, which can greatly reduce the overall cost of your metal tile roof replacement. On the other hand, you do give up some personalization, since part of the appeal of tile roofs is being able to arrange them into totally unique patterns.

The end result of this roof installation is a roof that brings the durability of metal alongside the classic Florida look of tiles. But how do these compare to clay roofing tiles when it comes to performance? Let’s take a closer look and find out.
Performance of Metal Roofing Tiles vs. Clay Roofing Tiles
In roofing, it’s rarely true that one roofing material is “better” than another. More often, roofing materials have their own advantages and weaknesses. To see if a metal roof that looks like tile can compare to the real thing, let’s compare these roofing materials by durability, longevity, and price!
Metal vs. Clay Tile Durability
In Florida, we tend to look at three factors when determining durability. These factors are tied to the biggest roof killers in The Sunshine State: high winds, UV rays, and impact damage. To determine whether a metal roof that looks like tile or real clay roofing tiles has the best durability, we’ll compare them side-by-side in these areas.

First, let’s talk wind resistance. Clay roofing tiles can resist winds up to 150 mph. This strength keeps them in place even during major hurricanes. Metal roofing tiles can do even better though, with wind resistance as high as 180 mph. While metal roofing does slightly outperform clay tiles in wind resistance, you can expect both materials to hold up against most hurricanes.

As we’ve established, metal tiles hold up better against impact damage than clay tiles, which can shatter when struck. UV resistance is a very different story, however. Because clay is made of natural materials and isn’t artificially colored, it holds up very well against sun bleaching. And after being baked in a kiln, it’s very unlikely for the sun to damage clay roofing tiles by drying them out.

Metal roof tiles reflect UV rays via their protective stone granules. This does have its limits, though. Over the years, metal roofing tiles may start to bleach from sun exposure. The good news, however, is that these tiles can be repainted to resolve any aesthetic issues.
Longevity of Clay vs. Metal Roofing Tiles
When it comes to longevity, it’s tough to compete with clay roofing tiles. That’s because these tiles last for upwards of 50 years on average. And in the best-case scenario, a clay tile roof can last over a century with proper maintenance and timely repairs. This is a lot to live up to, even for a metal roof that looks like tile!

While metal roofing tiles are durable, they simply can’t last as long as clay roofing tiles. Contractors install metal roofs by screwing them down into your roof. This means that the fasteners are left exposed on top of your roof, where they slowly degrade over time. Metal roof maintenance and repairs can fix any damage, but even so, it’s rare for exposed fastener metal roofs to last longer than 40-50 years. While this is still a great lifespan, it just can’t compare with real clay tiles.
Cost of Metal Tiles vs. Clay Tiles


When it comes to a metal roof that looks like tile and the real thing, there is a big difference in cost. Earlier we noted that metal tiles come in strips. This makes them faster to install than clay tiles, which are applied one by one. Additionally, metal tiles are much faster to manufacture than clay tiles, resulting in lower manufacturing cost.

The end result is that metal roofing tiles are much more affordable than clay tiles. But by how much?

Metal roofing tiles cost between $7 and $15 per square foot. This isn’t a cheap material, but it’s much more affordable than clay tile roofs, which start at $12 per square foot and go as high as $21 per square foot, depending on the type of tile you choose. When looking for an affordable tile roof, metal is much more accessible than clay!

### How Much Does It Cost to Replace Roof Shingles?

When planning a roof replacement, it’s normal to look for a reliable price online. But the cost to replace roof shingles is more complicated to calculate than many homeowners realize. That’s why the best thing you can do to find out how much your shingle roof replacement will cost is to get a free roofing quote.

That’s not a satisfying answer though, is it? We’re PITCH Roofing, and while we want you to get an estimate with us, we want you to have good shingle roof pricing information even more. That’s why we’re covering the full scope of the cost to replace roof shingles, so you can know what to expect when getting shingle roof quotes. Stick with us as we cover shingle roofing costs in Florida!
The Average Cost to Replace Roof Shingles in Florida


If you want a quick and easy number, the average cost to replace a shingle roof in Florida is about $13,000. Quick and easy numbers aren’t the same thing as reliable numbers, though. The cost to replace roof shingles is highly individualized to your roof and your choices, so let’s talk about the factors that are going to influence your final roof replacement price.
The Cost of Asphalt Roofing Shingles
Naturally, a large chunk of your roof replacement costs will go to materials. But which type of asphalt shingles you choose won’t just impact your budget. It will also change how long your shingle roof lasts and how much you spend on maintenance and repairs across its lifetime.

For many years, 3-tab shingles were the default shingle roofing material. Made of a thin baseboard and a layer of asphalt, these shingles are cheap to produce, but not nearly durable enough for Florida roofing. With wind resistance of only 70 mph, these shingles don’t hold up well even against tropical storms, let alone hurricanes. And while they’re extremely affordable at $1 to $3 per square foot, you’ll end up paying more in the long run with frequent repairs and a shorter lifespan, since these roofs rarely last longer than 15 years.

For all of these reasons, most Floridians have made the switch to architectural asphalt shingles. These shingles are made using fiberglass baseboards and multiple coatings of asphalt, which makes them much more durable with a wind resistance of up to 120 mph. Additionally, they’re topped with stone granules to resist damage from impact damage and UV rays.

But how much do they cost? The cost to replace roof shingles is slightly higher with architectural shingles, but still entirely affordable. You can expect to pay $3 to $7 in material costs for architectural shingles. They’re well worth the investment though, especially when you consider the reduced shingle roof repair costs and the longer lifespan of 20-25 years.
How Roof Features Affect Shingle Roof Replacement Costs
In addition to your choice of material, the specific features of your roof can inflate your roof replacement costs. Think of it this way: every unique feature on your roof is another thing that contractors have to work around when installing your new shingles. Licensed roofers should have no problem doing the work, but it will make the job take longer, which increases your labor costs.

What kinds of things can raise the cost to replace roof shingles, though? We’re talking about roof features like:

 	Chimneys
 	Skylights
 	Multiple hills or valleys
 	Dormer windows
 	Satellite dishes and antennas
 	Solar panels

Any and all of these features will increase your total roof replacement costs, so it’s a good idea to account for these before drawing up your roofing budget!
The Value of Roof Accessibility
Many homeowners are surprised to learn how much roof accessibility affects roofing costs. But it’s true — the easier you make it to get on and off your roof, the less you’ll pay for a new shingle roof. This is similar to accounting for unique roofing features since the increased cost reflects the extra time needed to access your roof.

Some of these factors are within your control. For example, you’ll usually need to clear your driveway so that your roofers can have a dumpster delivered to deposit your old roof into. Additionally, we strongly recommend clearing your yard of any debris or lawn ornaments so that contractors can more easily and directly access your roof.

Some things can’t be changed at the last moment, however. For example, if you have extensive landscaping features like large sections of plants or thick shrubs around your home, roofers may have to take extra time to avoid interfering with them.

One of the biggest ways accessibility can affect the cost to replace roof shingles is with your roof’s steepness. Specifically, if your roof’s pitch is steeper than 6:12, it will likely cost more to replace. That’s because especially steep roofs require special safety gear to access, which takes additional time to set up and requires more experienced labor. If your roof has an especially steep pitch, it’s likely that you’ll pay more for a shingle roof replacement!
Contractors With Lower Costs to Replace Roof Shingles


The roofers you pick will definitely impact how much your roof costs. Obviously this applies to scam roofers or less than honest roofers who inflate their prices. But even among honest, licensed roofing contractors, who you pick can have a huge impact on the cost to replace roof shingles on your home.

That’s because different roofing companies have different overhead costs. National roofers, for example, have to pay a lot more money to fund their large-scale operations. The only way they can afford this is by charging more for their roofing services, which means you end up paying more.

Local roofers like PITCH, however, are a very different story. Since we only operate locally, we have a smaller staff and much lower overhead costs. This means we can afford to offer you the best deals! When you add in the value of local roofing experts working on your roof, it’s clear that choosing local roofers is the right call in almost every situation.

### When to Replace a Shingle Roof in Florida

In Florida, there are lots of reasons that you might need to replace a shingle roof. Wear and tear, UV rays, and hurricane-force winds are just a few of the most common factors. Knowing the dangers to your roof is great, but how do you know when to replace a shingle roof?

If you want answers, you’re in the right place. We’re PITCH Roofing, your local roofing partners. Today we’re talking about the signs that you need to replace your shingle roof. Keep reading for our advice on spotting shingle roof damage in Florida!
7 Ways to Know When to Replace Your Shingle Roof


In figuring out when to replace a shingle roof, it helps to know the signs that your roof has been severely damaged. This can be tricky to differentiate from minor damage that only requires repair work. But with this list, we’ll make sure you’re ready to identify signs you need a new roof in Florida!
1. Cracked, Curled, or Missing Shingles
Having one or two damaged or missing shingles isn’t a sign that you need a new roof. Most contractors can install shingles quickly and without much fuss. However, recognizing a larger issue is a great way to know when to replace a shingle roof.

In Florida, two big roof killers are UV rays and high winds. The sun’s rays can cause shingles to dry up and crack or curl, which makes them ineffective at protecting your structure. Additionally, hurricane-force winds can tear shingles from your roof. A good rule of thumb is that if a quarter or more of your shingles are damaged or missing, it’s time to replace your roof.

You technically can repair damage of this size, but since roofing problems compound on themselves, it’s almost always safer and cheaper to just replace the roof all at once.
2. Granules in Your Gutters
You’re probably used to clearing leaves and other debris out of your gutters, but finding stone granules there is a big sign that your roof is reaching the end of its life. That’s because those granules serve an important function on your shingles: reflecting UV rays and helping resist impact damage. Without this protection, your roof is vulnerable to the Florida elements.

In most cases, granules won’t just come off during a storm. More often, they come off when your roof has reached an age where there’s no solution but to replace it. If you’re unsure when to replace a shingle roof, check your gutters and downspouts for granules. Finding them means it’s time for a roof replacement!
3. Dark Streaks on Your Roof
Have you ever noticed dark streaks on a shingle roof? This isn’t just regular dirt or staining — it’s actually algae growth. And it’s a classic sign of when to replace a shingle roof. Most new shingles come equipped with technology to minimize algae and mold growth, so dark stains could mean that your roof is reaching the end of its lifespan.

By itself, algae is not dangerous to your roof. However, there is no easy way to remove it. While it can be somewhat cleaned with a mixture of bleach and water, it likely won’t go away entirely. This, alongside the fact that older roofs are at higher risk of algae development, means that roof replacement is a great solution for dark staining on your roof.
4. Persistent Roof Leaks


A roof leak, by itself, is not a sign that you need a new roof. Several different leaks, or leaks that won’t go away, however, are big indicators that it’s time to consider replacement. In fact, multiple leaks throughout a home is one of the classic signs we look for when determining when to replace a shingle roof.

If you’ve already had a leak repaired and it either came back or another one started somewhere else in your home, that’s a sure sign that your roof can no longer effectively keep water out of your home. Alternatively, if you’ve only got one week but have gone months without repairing it, it’s probably time to replace your roof. Water damage spreads exponentially over time, and the only solution is new decking to support your shingles.
5. Your Neighbors Are Getting Roof Replacements
Following the crowd isn’t always the right move, but it can be a good way to know when to replace a shingle roof. Across Florida, most communities are built all at once. This means that their roofs are roughly the same age. So if you see several of your neighbors replacing their roofs, it probably means that you’re due for a new one as well.

There are exceptions, of course, and you should verify the age of your roof before having it replaced. But when everyone else’s roof starts hitting replacement age, it’s a reliable indicator that yours will hit that milestone soon!
6. Vegetation Growing on Your Roof
Algae stains may not be dangerous to your roof, but vegetation growing is a serious sign that you need a roof replacement ASAP. Moss and other plant life can quickly wear down your shingles, and the fact that they’re growing at all indicates that your roof is already damaged.

If your roof is 15 years old or younger, you can probably resolve this issue with a professional roof cleaning service if you act quickly. If you delay or if your roof is older, however, then your best bet is likely replacing your roof.
7. Your Roof Is Too Old
Good maintenance and timely roof repairs can do a lot to help your roof last a long time. But there is no repair that can fix your roof’s old age. In Florida, architectural shingles can last for about 20-25 years. If your roof is older than that, there’s no solution but to get it replaced.

Many homeowners wonder if they need to get a roof replacement if their roof isn’t showing any issues. And the answer is yes. Even without leaks or other roof problems, your homeowners insurance won’t cover a roof that has outlived its expected lifespan, because that roof likely can’t protect you from hurricanes. By getting a new roof, you can stay in good standing with your insurer and protect your home from the next major storm that blows through your neighborhood!

### Roof Replacement vs Reroofing: Which Is Right for Your Florida Home?

When you need a new roof, you have a lot of important decisions to make. This doesn’t just mean choosing what kind of shingles you want. Before you get to that step, homeowners need to weigh the pros and cons of a roof replacement vs. reroofing.

We’re PITCH Roofing, and as your local roofing partner, we’re here to help you make this crucial decision. Because between roof replacement and reroofing, there is no “better” option. It all comes down to which one is the best fit for your property and situation. To help you figure out which is right for you, let’s take a deep dive into both!
Roof Replacement vs. Reroofing: Definitions


The first step in deciding between a roof replacement and reroofing is establishing which is which. A roof replacement is exactly what it sounds like — contractors tear off your old shingles, replace your water-resistant underlayment and any damaged roof decking, then install your new shingle roof. This gets you a clean slate with a completely new roofing system!

Reroofing gets you a new roof as well, but in a different way. Instead of tearing off your old roof, contractors will nail in shingles over your existing roof. This means you’ll have two layers of shingles protecting your home, and you can expect a faster, cheaper installation process since roofers won’t have to tear off and dispose of your old roofing system.

This covers the basic definitions of your roof installation options. But when deciding between roof replacement vs. reroofing, it’s important to know the benefits of both options. Let’s compare these methods so you can see which one will best suit your home!
Choosing Between Roof Replacement and Reroofing


Both roof replacements and reroofing jobs have their ups and downs. Where one option has a weakness, the other has a strength. To decide which is right for your home, it’s important to look at the good and the bad so you have the full picture of what this decision will mean for your roof installation and the life of your roof going forward.
Reroofing Is Cheaper Than Roof Replacement
With roof replacements, tearing off your old roof takes a good deal of time and effort. Not only do roofing companies have to pay labor costs for that work, but they also have to rent a dumpster and have it delivered to your property. By skipping this step, you can save a substantial amount of money by choosing to reroof.

As we compare the costs of a roof replacement vs. reroofing, though, how much of a difference does this decision make? Specifics will always vary from job to job, but generally, it costs about $1 per square foot of your roof to tear off your old shingles. Factor in the cost of new decking and a new underlayment, and you’re potentially looking at several thousands of dollars in savings by choosing to reroof.
Roof Replacement Lasts Longer Than Reroofing
In Florida, high-quality asphalt shingles can last you for about 25 years. This is great, long-term protection from our infamous hurricanes. But you can only count on this kind of protection if you invest in a roof replacement. Otherwise, you’ll likely find that your roof doesn’t last as long.

This is because a roof replacement gives your roof a clean slate. Any existing problems are wiped clean, which creates a good base for your shingles. However, when you choose to reroof, your roof will only last for 15 years on average. This difference is because your old roofing system is still there, and while reroofing can extend that lifespan, it can’t completely reset the clock.
Reroofing Isn’t Suitable for Every Roof
In addition to deciding between roof replacement vs. reroofing, you’ll also need to determine if reroofing is even an option for your home. For example, your home can only have one layer of shingles on it if you want to reroof. Having more than two total layers of shingles goes against building codes and could put too much weight on your roofing system.

Additionally, some roofs aren’t in good enough shape for reroofing. If your roof has persistent leaks, for example, they could be due to problems with your decking. Adding more weight onto damaged decking won’t fix your issue, and in the worst case, it could lead to roof sagging. For this reason, it can be a good idea to get a roof inspection before reroofing if you’re seeing issues with your current roofing system.

When you sign up for a free, no-obligation estimate, we’ll be happy to prepare estimates for both a roof replacement and reroofing so you can compare your options side by side.
