FAQs About Roof Replacements and Reroofing in Florida
Q: Is reroofing a good idea for my roof?

A: Reroofing is a good option when your roof has minor damage, no underlying structural issues, and only one layer of shingles. It can also be a good idea if you need to save money on getting a new roof.

Q: Can I reroof with any roofing material?

A: No, reroofing can only be done over shingles, and it’s usually done by installing new shingles. However, you can also install a metal roof over an old shingle roof if the roof is otherwise suitable for reroofing.

Q: Can I finance a reroofing job?

A: Yes, you can finance reroofing. The process is the same and starts with applying for roof financing.

Q: Can I DIY a reroofing or roof replacement?

A: No, it is not a good idea to DIY any kind of roof installation. Not only could this be unsafe for you and your property, but it could also void warranties and lead to losing your homeowners insurance coverage.

Q: Will reroofing improve my home’s energy efficiency?

A: Yes, adding a second layer of shingles to your home improves insulation and keeps cool air in your home. However, getting a roof replacement can also improve your home’s energy efficiency by installing new shingles and vents.

### Rolled Rubber Roofing for Residential & Commercial Properties

In Florida, flat roofing is a big part of both residential and commercial roofing. But what you put on your flat roof will determine how well it protects your structure. For this reason, more and more Floridians are choosing rolled rubber roofs to keep their roofs secure and leak-free.

We’re PITCH Roofing, your local flat roofing experts. Follow along with us today as we cover what a rolled rubber roof is, how much it costs, and whether it’s the right fit for your roof. We’ve got all the information you need to know ahead of your flat roof replacement!
What Is a Rolled Rubber Roof?


Before we talk about rubber roofs, we have to talk about flat roofs in general. Unlike sloped roofs, flat roofs are highly prone to standing water. While they theoretically have a slight slope to help water move off your roof, in severe storms there can still be temporary water pooling on your flat roof. When this happens, it helps to have strong, resilient rubber to keep the water out.

The name “rolled rubber roof” refers to both the composition and installation method of this roofing material. Rubber roofing often refers to TPO, thermoplastic polyolefin. This is a new roofing technology made from rubberized polymers, which create a watertight barrier across your flat roof.

We call these rolled rubber roofs because of how they’re applied to your roof. As a single-ply roofing membrane, contractors roll out TPO roofing sheets across your flat roof. They then heat-weld the seams to your roof to ensure that no water can get in.

The result is a rolled rubber roof that can keep your roof dry and secure even through the worst of Florida’s weather. But how much does TPO roofing cost? Let’s talk about how much you can expect to pay for a rubber roof.
How Much Does a Rubber Roof Cost?
Rubber roofing costs can be complicated to calculate. While we can tell you that the average cost of a rolled rubber roof is $7,500 to $13,500 for a 1,500-square-foot flat roof, that doesn’t necessarily mean that’s how much you’ll pay for your roof. For that, we need to get a little more specific.

Naturally, the size of your roof influences your total flat roofing costs. TPO roofing costs $5 to $9 per square foot, so in theory, you can have a rough idea of your roofing costs by applying the square footage of your roof to these numbers. The reality is a little more tricky, though.

For example, roof accessibility has a big impact on your roof replacement costs. Installing a rolled rubber roof becomes much harder if roofers can’t easily get onto your roof due to shrubs or debris in your yard. Unique factors like this — as well as skylights, chimneys, and other unique roofing factors — will have a major impact on your total rubber roof costs.

Additionally, which roofers you pick will determine your overall job costs. National roofers, for instance, cost more than hiring local contractors. This isn’t just because of corporate greed, but because national roofing chains have massive overhead costs to support their large-scale operations. Locally owned and operated roofing companies don’t have these costs, so we’re able to offer a much more affordable flat roof replacement cost.

At the end of the day, the best way to find out how much your rolled rubber roof will cost is to start collecting roofing quotes. Before we get to that step, though, we should first decide if a rubber roof is a good fit for your home or commercial property. To do that, we have to look at the good and the bad of TPO roofing.
Pros and Cons of a Rolled Rubber Roof


Every roof has some good and bad qualities. And while rubber roofs are a top-of-the-line flat roofing style, they aren’t perfect, either. To see if TPO could be the roofing material for you, let’s take an in-depth look at the pros and cons!
Pro: Great Longevity
When you invest in a rolled rubber roof, you want it to last. And that’s exactly what you get with TPO roofing. This technology hit the roofing market in the 90s, so we’re still learning exactly how long it can last. But the expectation across the industry is that TPO roofs will last for 20-30 years, even in Florida. For a flat roofing material, this is a long, full life!
Con: Aging Seams
Florida is called The Sunshine State for a reason. And while all of those UV rays make for great beach days, they aren’t quite so nice to your rolled rubber roof. With a rubberized roof, the sun’s rays can eventually wear down your roofing material. This is especially common with TPO seams, which can degrade under the heat of the sun.

Luckily, fixing this issue is fairly easy. And it will take your roof years to develop issues like this. Still, you should plan to address them if you choose to invest in TPO roofing!
Pro: Low Maintenance
While TPO seams are a weak point, the roof generally needs very little maintenance. Common flat roofing issues like mold growth and puncture damage are very unlikely when you invest in a rolled rubber roof. TPO has high tensile strength and doesn’t have any crevices for mold to develop in, which makes it great at standing up to most of Florida’s weather patterns.

### The 10 Best Roofing Materials for Floridians in 2025

When looking at your roof replacement options, it’s easy to feel overwhelmed. There are a lot of roofing materials out there, and figuring out which one is right for you can be tough if you don’t have a background in roofing. That’s why PITCH Roofing is here to give a comprehensive breakdown of the 10 roof types you should know about.

As licensed Florida roofers, nobody knows local roofing options better than us. Today we’re going to explore the different types of roofs, giving you crucial information like how long they last, what they’re made of, and how much they cost. Keep reading for our full guide on Florida roofing options in 2025!
Roof Types by Material


Before you get far in the roofing process, you’ll have to commit to a material. But this is a major decision that will have lasting impacts on your property and your finances. That’s why you need to be completely informed before committing to any material!

To get you there, let’s talk about the 10 most popular roof types in Florida.
Shingle Roofing
Shingles are by far the most popular roofing material in Florida in 2025 and any other year. They’re more diverse than most people realize, though. Asphalt shingles are the most common, made with a mat of fiberglass coated in asphalt and then topped with protective stone granules.

Synthetic shingles are also an excellent way of protecting your home and giving it a great aesthetic, however. Made of recycled rubber and plastic, these shingles offer an entirely different experience. To help you decide what roof type works best for your home or commercial property, let’s look at the different types of shingles.
Asphalt Architectural Shingles
Durable and affordable, architectural shingles are the most popular roofing material in North America. They last for 20 to 25 years, and they’re capable of withstanding winds up to 110 mph. At a price point of $5 to $9 per square foot for roof installation, these shingles are a great, budget-friendly roofing material.
Luxury Asphalt Shingles
Think of luxury shingles as an even more upgraded version of architectural shingles. They offer a unique, luxurious aesthetic, and their thicker composition gives them extra wind resistance and durability. Luxury asphalt shingles cost $8 to $17 per square foot and last for up to 40 years.
Synthetic Shingles
Also called composite shingles, these unique shingles replicate the look of slate or wood shake roofing at a fraction of the cost. These high-end shingles last for about 50 years in Florida and cost $7 to $14 per square foot on average.
Tile Roofing
Tile roofs have been a Florida staple since the time of the earliest Spanish settlers. Made of overlapping tiles, these roofing systems seamlessly move water off your roof while creating a gorgeous, timeless aesthetic. And with many different types of tiles available, you can create virtually any style you can imagine.

The biggest choice you’ll make with this roof type, though, is what it’s made of. Let’s look at your tile roofing options!
Clay Roofing Tiles
Of all the roof types in Florida, these last the longest. Made of baked clay, these tiles can last for up to 100 years with proper maintenance, and you can count on getting at least 50 years of protection. Throw in great wind and water resistance, and it’s not hard to see why clay tiles have been popular in Florida for centuries. They come at a high cost, though: $12 to $21 per square foot.
Concrete Roofing Tiles
These tiles are made of concrete that has been painted the color of clay tiles. It’s hard for laymen to tell the difference, although concrete tiles only last about 50 years on average. They’re much cheaper to install though, at only $9 to $19 per square foot.
Metal Roofing
Metal roofing is on the rise in The Sunshine State going into 2025. That’s not only because the look is becoming more popular, but as homeowners prioritize hurricane protection, metal roofing stands as one of the best ways to safeguard your property.

To see if metal roofing is right for you, let’s talk about the different metal roof types in Florida.
Exposed Fastener Metal Roofs
Metal roofing systems with corrugated panels that are drilled down onto your roof are called exposed fastener metal roofs. These are affordable at only $7 to $12 per square foot, but they only last 30-45 years because their exposed fasteners can weather under the harsh Florida sun. Still, they’re a great option for affordable metal roofing!
Standing Seam Metal Roofs
Metal roofs with hidden fasteners are called standing seam. With these roofs, the fasteners attach beneath the roofing panel, protecting it from the elements. This increases installation costs to $10 to $35 per square foot, but it also raises the average lifespan of your roof to 50-70 years. With a sleek, smooth exterior, these roofs are very popular among Florida homeowners.
Stone-Coated Steel Roofs
Stone-coated steel is just what it sounds like: sheets of steel roofing coated in a protective, rust-resistant alloy and a thick layer of stone granules. These roofing sheets can then be formed into either metal shingles or metal tiles, offering two very different aesthetics. With either option, you can expect to pay $7 to $15 per square foot for up to 70 years of protection.
Flat Roofing
Flat roofs have a unique set of challenges to overcome. Namely, they have to prevent standing water from leaking into low-slope roofing systems without becoming worn out by the harsh Florida elements. This is a tall order, but there are several flat roof types that are up to the task.

Now, let’s look at the different flat roofing options at your disposal!
Modified Bitumen
Made of rubberized asphalt, modified bitumen is great at keeping out water and standing up to Florida’s harsh UV rays. With high tensile strength, mod bit roofs last about 20 years and only cost $4 to $8 per square foot. Roofing doesn’t get much more affordable than this!
TPO Roofing
TPO, thermoplastic polyolefin, is a new arrival on the roofing scene, but it’s making big waves. A single-ply roofing system, this thin layer of rubber polymers has unmatched water resistance to withstand any water pooling on your low-slope roof. These roofs cost $4 to $10 per square foot and last for 20 to 30 years on average.

### How Much Does Gutter Replacement Cost in Florida?

Florida may be The Sunshine State, but we see a lot of rain, especially in the summers. Healthy gutters are essential to keeping that rainwater away from your structure’s foundations. So when a storm or wear and tear damages your current gutters, it’s essential to get help right away. Price is always an issue, though, so many homeowners are asking, how much does gutter replacement cost?

Well, we can tell you that new gutter installation costs average around $1,300 to $3,300 when replacing an entire gutter system for a 1,700-square-foot home. That’s a big range, though, and depending on the specifics of your home, you could end up with very different gutter replacement costs.

We’re PITCH Roofing, and today we’re giving you a foolproof guide to gutter installation costs in Florida!
Signs You Need New Gutters


Before we get too far into gutter replacement costs, it’s important to first establish when you need new gutters. Sometimes it’s obvious, but other times, homeowners aren’t sure whether they need gutter repairs or a complete gutter replacement of the whole system.

That’s why we’re going to help you identify when you need new gutters. Some of the biggest signs that you need to have your entire guttering system replaced include:

 	Gutters that have fallen away from your home due to wear and tear or hurricane-force winds
 	Substantial rust throughout your gutters and downspouts
 	Holes or cracks appearing throughout your gutter system
 	Gutters that retain water even when cleared of debris

If one or more of these scenarios sounds familiar, then there’s a good chance that your entire guttering system needs to be removed and replaced with new, healthy gutters. If you’re still unsure, you can always schedule a roof inspection to determine the extent of repairs that your roof needs!

Now that we’ve covered how to tell if you need new gutters, let’s talk about how much that can cost.
2025 Gutter Replacement Cost Factors in Florida
While everyone wants a quick, easy number, the average gutter replacement cost is not the most reliable. That’s because your home may not be the “average.” It may be larger or smaller, or you may want a different gutter material, or any number of other factors.

2. Size and Accessibility of Your Roof


Naturally, the larger your roof, the more guttering material you need. This increases both material costs and labor costs for the extra installation work. But when it comes to calculating your gutter replacement costs, square footage is far from the only consideration.

For example, multi-story structures often have higher gutter installation costs than single-story residences. You’d be surprised how much which roofers you choose can change your gutter replacement costs. This isn’t just that underhanded contractors get greedy (although there’s some truth to that). But more often, the issue is that different gutter replacement companies have different overheads.

### Pros, Cons, and Costs of Terracotta Roofing Tiles in Florida

Terracotta roofing tiles first arrived in Florida with some of the earliest Spanish settlers. And ever since, these hardy tiles have been a mainstay of Florida roofing. But after centuries of advancements in roofing technology, can they compete on the modern roofing market?

That’s what we’re here to find out. We’re PITCH Roofing, and as licensed Florida roofers, we know a thing or two about local tile roofing. Follow along with us as we cover terracotta tile roofing and whether it’s the right fit for your Florida home!
What Are Terracotta Roofing Tiles?


To start making terracotta roofing tiles, manufacturers first fill tile molds with wet clay. This simple production method allows manufacturers to create clay roofing tiles in nearly any shape or size. Once they’ve poured the clay into the molds, the clay is then hardened by heat-treating it in a kiln. The result is a strong, thick roofing material in the shape of your preferred tile.

Depending on how long your tile is baked for, it can be more or less thick and heavy. The bake time also influences the feel and finish of your tiles. Creating the classic terracotta finish, though, is enough to create a strong, resilient tile that’s ready to withstand Florida’s weather patterns.

Over the years, Florida roofers have learned how to make the best use of terracotta roofing tiles. By strategically placing and layering tiles on your roof, they can create a water-resistant barrier that helps guide water off your roof without allowing it to penetrate into your home.

This covers the basics of what clay roofing tiles are, but there are still plenty of unanswered questions. Let’s get you those answers by looking at the good and bad of tile roofing!
Terracotta Roofing Tiles in Florida - Video
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jRkNkRFV7T0
Pros and Cons of Terracotta Roofing Tiles in Florida
Every climate has its unique quirks and roofing requirements. That’s especially true in Florida, where our roofs need to be hurricane-ready. As we look at the pros and cons of terracotta roofing tiles, we’re going to focus on the needs and concerns of real Florida homeowners like you.

Without further ado, let’s delve into everything you need to know to determine if these roofing tiles are right for you!
Pro: Built to Last
Every homeowner wants a roof that will last a long time, and there is no better option than terracotta roofing tiles. In fact, their great longevity is why the core principles behind clay tile roofing haven’t changed in centuries. But how long do these roofs last, exactly?

Clay tile roofs average around 50 years. This is a great lifespan for a Florida roof, but it’s not what makes them exceptional. The reason these roofs are special is that terracotta roofing tiles can last for up to 100 years or more with proper tile roof maintenance. This is an unbeatable figure, even when compared to new technologies like metal roofing.
Con: Underlayments Need Replacing


A water-resistant underlayment is a crucial part of any clay tile roofing system. This barrier sits on top of your decking but below your terracotta roofing tiles. The idea is that when the occasional bit of water sneaks past your tiles, your water-resistant barrier will be there to catch it and keep your vulnerable decking safe and dry.

And this system works great! The only problem is that underlayments don’t last as long as terracotta roofing tiles. In fact, most insurance companies will require you to replace your underlayment about every 20 years. Otherwise, the underlayment could degrade and leave your roof unprotected.

If you have a clay tile roof, this puts you in an odd position. Contractors will have to remove your tiles, replace the underlayment, and then re-install your tile roof. This is much cheaper than a roof replacement because you don’t have to buy new tiles, but it’s still worth nothing that this is an expense you’ll want to plan for when you choose terracotta roofing tiles.
Pro: Hurricane-Ready Protection
When compared to asphalt shingles, terracotta roofing tiles offer greatly enhanced roof protection. Some of the best protective features of clay tiles include:

 	Class 4 impact rating, which protects against damage from hail and storm debris
 	Wind resistance up to 150 mph, enough to withstand major hurricanes
 	Class A fire rating, the best available
 	Rot- and pest-resistant to prevent any roof infestations

With Florida’s unpredictable weather, there is no such thing as a truly “Florida-proof” roof. However, terracotta roofing tiles come pretty close. With this kind of robust protection, you can count on a clay tile roof to keep your home safe, both during hurricane season and throughout the rest of the year!
Con: High Installation Costs
While you’ll hear a lot of people rave about the high quality of their terracotta roofing tiles, you won’t hear anyone saying that they’re cheap. In fact, clay roofing tiles are a luxury roofing material, meaning they come with especially high installation costs.

Roofing prices will always vary from case to case. But on average, terracotta roofing tiles cost $12 to $21 per square foot. If your roof is the average size of 1,700 square feet, that means a new clay tile roof will cost you $20,400 to $35,700. While the installation costs are high, many Florida homeowners feel it’s worth it for the long-term protection of their homes!
Pro: Eco-Friendly Roofing
Did you know that asphalt shingles take up a massive amount of space in landfills? The latest estimates suggest that every year, Americans dump 20 billion tons of asphalt shingles into landfills. As space for dumping becomes more and more scarce, many homeowners want a way to reduce their ecological footprints.

Terracotta roofing tiles are a great solution. Clay is 100% natural, so these tiles are easy to recycle. This means no more space added to landfills! Additionally, clay doesn’t produce any harmful chemicals in the kiln, so there’s virtually no pollution in the manufacturing process. This makes clay tile roofs very popular among Florida homeowners looking to go green.

### Are Metal Roof Tiles Right for Your Florida Home?

Tile roofing has been part of Florida's history since the earliest European settlers. And for years, new advancements in roofing technology have kept tile roofing strong and durable enough to remain competitive on the roofing market. Now, there's a new update to give your roof long-lasting security and a classic aesthetic: metal roof tiles.

Metal roofing tiles are an exciting new technology, but are they right for your roof? We're PITCH Roofing, and today, we're helping you answer that question. As experienced Florida roofing contractors, we've got the know-how and expertise to cover both the good and the bad of metal roof tiles. Before we dive into the pros and cons, though, there's an even more important question to answer: What are metal tile roofs?
What Are Metal Roof Tiles?


Historically, tile roofs have come in several different material types, although clay and concrete are the most popular. And contrary to popular belief, metal roof tiles are not just metal roofing sheets that have been shaped into roofing tiles. So if they aren't a normal tile material, and they aren't completely metal, what are they?

Metal roof tiles are a kind of stone-coated steel roofing. In the manufacturing process, manufacturers start by shaping the roofing sheets into the shape of tiles. Unlike individual tiles, though, these are created as panels of several tiles, which makes for faster (and thus less expensive) installation. From there, the panels are coated in a protective, corrosion-resistant alloy. This helps prevent rust and other premature aging from affecting your metal tiles!

The final step in the manufacturing process is applying the protective stone granules. This addition serves a few key functions. First, it allows you to give your metal roof the classic tile look. This includes having a natural clay tile color, either the classic tile red or more natural, neutral tones.

These tones aren't just decorative, though; they also offer great protection. Stone granules help reflect UV light away from your home, which lessens the effects of a major roof stressor. Additionally, they're an extra layer of protection against impact damage from storm debris or hail. This gives metal roof tiles a big leg up on clay tiles, which are more brittle and can crack or shatter when struck by flying objects.

No roofing material is the perfect fit for every home, though. To help you decide if metal tile roofs are right for you, let's delve into the good and bad of metal tile roofs!
Pros & Cons of Metal Roof Tiles


When deciding on something as important as a roof replacement, it's essential to weigh the good and the bad. As we do this, though, keep in mind that there's no such thing as a "perfect roof." With that said, let's get started on some of homeowners' favorite and least favorite features of metal roof tiles!
Pro: Metal Roofing Durability
Metal roof tiles have the charming aesthetic of tiles, but the full-coverage protection of metal roofing. What does that mean in terms of keeping your roof safe, though? With a metal tile roof, your roof will enjoy protection like:

 	Wind resistance up to 165 mph — more than enough to withstand even major hurricanes!
 	UV resistance to keep your roof from experiencing premature wear and tear.
 	Class A fire resistance.
 	Rust and corrosion resistance thanks to protective anti-corrosion alloys.
 	Resistance to pests and mold growth, two big problems in humid Florida.

All of these factors come together to create comprehensive protection for your home. While clay tiles are also a durable roofing material, nothing can beat metal roofing when it comes to durability. No roof is 100% "Florida proof," but metal roofing tiles certainly come close!
Con: Exposed Fasteners
Installing metal roof tiles is, all things considered, pretty easy. During your roof replacement, contractors will drill down the tile panels straight into your roof. In this way, your roof's fasteners sit on top of the metal roofing panel. And for the most part, this installation method will do a great job keeping your roof secure against wind uplift and pests. There can be issues with how exposed fasteners age, however.

Since your fasteners sit on top of your roof, they're exposed to the Florida elements year-round. This means they're dealing with high winds, UV rays, and rain. These kinds of roof stressors take a toll! Over time, your fasteners can rust and corrode, even with anti-corrosion alloys. This can lead to serious roofing problems if not addressed quickly.

That's why we strongly recommend biennial roof inspections for anyone getting an exposed fastener metal roofing system. By getting regular roof inspections, you can stay ahead of roofing problems and keep your overall roofing costs down. Because with roofs, repairs only get more expensive over time!
Pro: Long-Term Protection
In addition to being durable, metal roofs last for a long time. Remember all those protective features we mentioned? They translate to a long lifetime for your metal roof tiles. Even with the problems with exposed fasteners, metal tile roofs still last much longer than the 20 or so years you get with asphalt shingles.

In Florida, our metal roofs can last anywhere from 40 to 70 years. With exposed fastener metal roofs like these, though, you're looking at 40-50 years on average. When you consider the overall value of a durable roofing system like this, though, this is still a great lifespan.
Con: Not Suited for Florida's Coasts
In most climates, metal roof tiles hold up great. There is one notable exception, though: coastal areas. That's because coastal waters have a high salt content, and as that salt gets into the air, it can greatly accelerate rust and corrosion. For this reason, most metal roofs on the coast need to be made of aluminum to prevent rust.

The good news, though, is that metal tile roofs perform well in most of Florida, even with us sandwiched between the Gulf of Mexico and the Atlantic. If you're five miles or more from the coastline, then you're far enough away that your roof shouldn't be in any increased danger of rusting.
Pro: Affordable Compared to Clay Tiles
It's not often that you hear about metal roofing as an affordable option. But with metal roof tiles, it's true! Because metal is easier and less costly to manufacture than clay tiles, your material costs with a metal tile roof replacement will be much lower than with clay roofing tiles.

Installation is faster with metal roof tiles, too. Since metal tiles come by the panel, they're much faster to install. And since metal roofs use exposed fastener roofing systems, they're simple and quick to drill into place. By keeping your roof replacement quick and simple, you can drastically reduce your labor costs.

So how much do metal roof tiles cost? Metal roof tiles cost between $7 and $15 per square foot. While this is more expensive than shingles, it's a huge discount compared to clay roofing tiles! This is still a large range when talking about roof replacement costs, though. For a more specific figure, you'll have to sign up for a free roofing quote.

### How Much Does Shingle Replacement Cost in Florida?

Asphalt shingles are the most widely used roofing material in Florida. And while these shingles are both cost-effective and durable, they can’t hold out against our severe local weather patterns forever. Sooner or later, every homeowner needs to know how much shingle replacement costs.

That’s what we’re here for! We’re PITCH Roofing, and as local shingle roofing experts, we’ve successfully completed more than our fair share of shingle roof repairs and replacements. Stick with us as we use this know-how to answer all of your questions about shingle roofing costs in Florida!
Shingle Roof Repair or Replacement?


The first question to ask when determining your shingle replacement costs is whether you need a handful of new shingles or an entirely new roof. As you might imagine, these two options come with very different price tags. Luckily, it’s usually pretty easy to tell the difference.

Signs you need a roof repair include:

 	Missing a small handful of shingles
 	Bent or dented flashing
 	Cracking or curling shingles
 	Minor, localized roof leaks
 	Moss or algae growth on your shingle

For any one of these issues, a small repair is usually enough to fix the issue and get your roof back to normal. On the other hand, a complete roof replacement will cost substantially more. Some of the indicators that you need a roof replacement are:

 	A roof that’s more than 20 years old, especially if its age is over 25 years
 	Missing large sections of shingles, especially if the underlayment is exposed
 	Finding stone granules in your gutters
 	Roof sagging
 	Large leaks with extensive water damage, including (but not limited to) ceiling stains
 	Higher than usual energy bills

More extensive roofing damage requires a bigger, more costly solution. As we take a look at shingle replacement costs in Florida, keep in mind whether you’re looking to replace a few shingles or to get an entirely new shingle roof!
Average Shingle Replacement Costs in Florida
Most shingle roofing problems can be fixed by just replacing a small handful of shingles. In terms of labor, this usually only includes tearing off any damaged shingles, patching or re-sealing any damaged underlayment, and installing new shingles. How much does a shingle replacement cost, though?

The good news is that most shingle roof repairs don’t cost much. In terms of material costs, even high-quality architectural shingles rarely cost more than five or six dollars per square foot. While labor costs usually make up 60% of any budget, these repairs are usually only a few hundred dollars. For many homeowners, it makes sense to choose a handyman roofer who doesn’t charge much for basic repair work.

On the other hand, some shingle repair jobs are more complicated. This is especially true when there is water damage, which may have gotten through to your roof decking. In this case, you may need a partial roof replacement, which includes your shingles, water-resistant underlayment, and decking.

These jobs tend to cost considerably more. The exact shingle replacement cost will vary depending on the extent of the damage. However, for a partial roof replacement, you can expect costs to range anywhere from $1,500 to $3,000. Once jobs get more expensive than that, it often makes more sense to simply replace the entire roof.

Now that we’ve covered shingle repair costs in Florida, it’s time to talk about what you can expect to pay if you need a complete roof replacement.
2025 Shingle Roof Replacement Costs


As we mentioned, asphalt shingles usually cost around five dollars at the most. However, this isn’t the only material cost factor to consider when discussing shingle roof replacement costs. Because when talking about a complete roofing system, there is much more to it than just asphalt shingles.

A complete roofing system includes:

 	Asphalt shingles
 	Roof flashing
 	Soffits and fascia
 	Ridge caps
 	Attic vents
 	Water-resistant underlayment
 	Healthy roof decking

When replacing a shingle roof, your contractors need to provide and install all of these essential parts of your roofing system. As you might imagine, these materials can drastically increase the total shingle replacement costs.

But replacing a roof is more than just providing materials. You’ll also need to pay for labor, which as we mentioned, usually adds about 60% to your total roofing costs. This number can be higher, though, particularly if you have an especially steep roof or there’s any difficulty accessing your roof. That’s why it’s best to make sure your yard is as clear as possible before your roofers show up!

So with all of this said, how much will a shingle roof replacement cost on average? When budgeting for a new shingle roof, you should expect to pay $5 to $9 per square foot. In Florida, the average size of a roof is around 1,700 square feet. So for a new shingle roof, the average Floridian will pay $8,500 to $15,300.

Average Shingle Roof Replacement Cost in 2025

To get a better idea of what factors will influence how much your shingle roof costs, let’s look at every step of the shingle roof replacement process and see what could raise or lower your total costs!
Costs to Remove Your Old Shingles
Before roofers can start installing your new shingles, they first have to remove your old ones. In general, this is quick work that doesn’t come with astronomical fees — usually less than a dollar per square foot of your roof. However, there are ways for your shingle roof replacement costs to increase even with this task.

This is where the pitch of your roof matters. If you have an especially steep roof, one with a pitch of 9:12 or steeper, tearing off your old roof suddenly becomes a lot harder. That’s because roofers may need special safety gear to safely move across your roof. This not only increases material and labor costs, but it also makes the job take longer.

It’s also a good idea to make sure that roofers can easily access your roof. If it’s hard for contractors to get on your roof, the whole job takes longer. This can mean a big bump in your labor costs!
Replacing Roof Decking
Your decking is the material (usually wood) that the rest of your roof sits on. Since it’s the basis of your roofing system, any damaged sections will need replacing after your contractors have removed your shingles. This is something of a wild card factor when it comes to your shingle roofing quote.

That’s because decking is the only part of a new roof that a shingle roof replacement cost estimate can’t cover. Why? Because there’s no way to be sure of how much decking needs replaced until your old shingles have been removed. While a roofer completing your estimate will give it their best guess based on signs of damage to your shingles, the only way to know for sure is to tear off your old roof and see what’s going on beneath it.

The good news is that roof decking is usually inexpensive. On average, expect to pay $2 to $5 per square foot for roof decking. And unless your roof has a history of major leaks and water damage, in all likelihood very little of your total roof decking will need replacing.
Installing Your New Roofing System
When we talk about your roofing system, we’re including everything. This means shingles, flashing, underlayment, soffits/fascia, and your venting system. This is where the bulk of your roofing costs come from. However, we don’t recommend lowering your shingle roof replacement cost by skimping on a quality roof installation.

When it comes to installing your roof, there are two extremely important factors: materials and labor. By investing in quality roofing materials (like architectural shingles) created by top-quality manufacturers (like Owens Corning), you can get a quality roofing system that will protect you from the Florida elements. ### 5 Roof Gutter Maintenance Tips to Follow

If you want to get as much life out of your roof as possible, keeping up on roof gutter maintenance is one of the best things you can do. But if you’re not used to caring for gutters, you may not know how best to care for them. That’s a problem, because gutters do essential work moving water off your roof and away from your foundation.

We’re PITCH Roofing, and as your local roofing partner, we’re happy to help you keep your roof in top condition. Nobody knows the value of a good, healthy roof like we do. So stick with us as we cover the most important ways that you can take care of your gutters and, by extension, your whole roofing system!
Roof Gutter Maintenance Tips for Florida Homeowners


Maintaining your gutters is important no matter where you live, but it’s even more essential in Florida. When a hurricane is at your front door, clogged or damaged gutters could lead to flooding on your roof, which is an expensive and dangerous problem to have.

But we’re not going to let that happen. Let’s talk about the easy roof gutter maintenance you can do to keep your home dry and protected!
1. Start a Gutter Cleaning Schedule
Most homeowners know that they need to clean out their gutters from time to time as part of essential roof gutter maintenance. Otherwise, palm fronds and leaves can accumulate and stop water from flowing to your downspouts. While homeowners usually know this, many only clear their gutters occasionally, which often leads to prolonged periods where it doesn’t happen simply because the homeowner gets busy and doesn’t remember.

The best solution is to set a regular gutter cleaning schedule so that you don’t forget. In Florida, we recommend scheduling gutter cleanings twice a year — once in the spring, and once in the fall. These seasons are when leaves are most often falling off our local trees, so it’s a good time to make sure your gutters are clean and still working.

As a homeowner, you can either pay to have your gutters cleaned or do it yourself. If you choose to clean your own gutters, you’ll want to use a gutter trowel to scoop out any debris. Once the gutters are clear of large debris, clean out the remnants with a hose, and your gutters should be good for another six months!
2. Consider Installing Gutter Guards
In most cases, cleaning out your gutters twice a year is enough to keep them working properly. But if there are many trees over your home, you may find yourself with more debris in your gutters than average. Alternatively, you may just find that cleaning your gutters is an annoying chore that you don’t want to do or spend money paying someone else to do.

In either case, gutter guards can be a great way to cut down on the burden of roof gutter maintenance. These protective devices cover your gutters to help prevent debris from entering in and clogging the system. It’s important to note that you still need to clean your gutters even with gutter guards. But they make the task easier and faster!

With gutter guards, you only need to brush the debris off of the guards. You don’t need a trowel for digging up debris or a hose to rinse out your gutters. You’ll also need to clean your gutters less often — roughly once a year. For a small investment in your home, you can massively cut back on the amount of work your roof gutter maintenance requires!
3. Regularly Inspect Your Gutters


Any time you’re cleaning your gutters is an opportunity to inspect them and see if you need to perform any other roof gutter maintenance. For example, cracks and holes can develop in your gutters over time. If you find them early, applying sealant can fix the issue and keep your gutters healthy for years to come.

Other times, you may notice larger issues, like your gutters starting to sag or lean away from your home. If this happens, it’s best to call in a professional to help. While you can try to straighten out or reattach your own gutters, any mistake could put your roof or your foundation in danger. For this reason, it’s best to leave the larger jobs to the pros rather than attempt DIY gutter maintenance!
4. Don’t Overlook Your Downspouts
Homeowners tend to focus on gutters, but your downspouts are just as important. If there’s an issue with your downspouts, even if your gutters are clear, then that water is going to end up exactly where you don’t want it: eating away at your foundation.

That’s why it’s important to regularly inspect your downspouts as part of routine roof gutter maintenance. Similar to gutters, you’ll want to look for cracks, holes, and rust. Additionally, it’s a good idea to check out your downspouts when it rains to make sure that water is coming where you want it.

If not, it could indicate that your downspouts are clogged. Just like debris can build up in your gutters, the same thing can happen with downspouts. In some cases, a hose will be enough to clear out debris. In others, though, you may want to use a shop vac at the base of your downspouts while gently shaking debris loose throughout the downspout.
5. Trim Trees Over Your Roof
This is an optional part of roof gutter maintenance, but it can make your life a lot easier. By regularly trimming any branches over your roof, you can greatly reduce the amount of debris that makes its way into your gutters. This means less frequent cleanings!

This is also a good habit to get into for general roof safety. Twigs and leaves on your roof can become a hotspot for pests, which can eventually start to make their way into your roof. Additionally, leaves or branches being whipped around by a storm can seriously damage your shingles. By regularly trimming palm fronds and tree branches over your home, you can protect your gutters and your roof as a whole!

While roof gutter maintenance can give your gutters the best chance at longevity, there’s no way to prevent every single issue. ### Metal Roof Installation Guide: Planning Your Roof Replacement

Planning a metal roof installation is a lot of work. With shingles it’s as simple as picking the color you want, but metal roofs require more consideration. What kind of material are you going to use? What style of metal roof do you want? Are you interested in metal shingles?

We understand: it’s a lot. That’s why PITCH Roofing is here to explain all of your metal roof replacement options. With tons of local roofing experience, we know what options are best suited to Florida homeowners. Keep reading for a breakdown of all your metal roofing options!
Metal Roof Installation Materials


When it comes to metal roofing in Florida, some options are better than others. For example, you won’t see any tin roofs around here because there are simply better materials available at a similar price point. So what are your options when planning your metal roof installation?

Let’s look at the three most popular metal roofing materials in Florida!
Galvanized Steel
Galvanized steel is the default choice for metal roofs. When it comes to durability and resilience, nothing beats a classic steel roofing system. Steel roofs resist water, wind, and even fire, ensuring that your home is protected in nearly any circumstance.

There is one small caveat, though. Galvanized steel is coated with zinc to help it resist rust damage. And if you don’t live near a large body of saltwater, then this is plenty of protection to keep your roof safe and rust-free. However, if you live within five miles of Florida’s coasts, this may not be the right material for you. Saltwater is especially corrosive to steel roofs, so you will need additional protection to secure your new metal roof.

If you live inland, though, there’s no reason that galvanized steel can’t keep your property safe. And since it’s one of the most affordable metal roofing materials, it’s extremely popular among homeowners who are worried about metal roof installation costs!
Galvalume Steel
Think of this as an upgraded version of the classic steel roof. Galvalume steel is a very special alloy that manufacturers apply to steel roofing panels. Made of both zinc and aluminum, Galvalume offers even better rust protection than galvanized steel. While it still isn’t the very best choice for coastal Floridians, it’s certainly much more resilient against Florida’s humidity than galvanized steel!

In all other areas, it offers the same reliable, durable protection that you expect with steel roofing. With its increased corrosion protection, Galvalume steel really is the ideal steel roof. While it’s a bit more costly than galvanized steel roofing, you can still get a moderately priced metal roof installation when you choose Galvalume!
Aluminum
If you’re committed to getting a roof that won’t corrode, aluminum is the way to go. This lightweight, durable roofing material is the go-to option for metal roof installations in coastal Florida. Aluminum doesn’t rust, and it resists corrosion better than nearly any other metal. So if you’re worried about preventing rust and corrosion, aluminum is more than capable of standing up to both saltwater and Florida’s infamous humidity.

Aluminum isn’t only great at rust resistance, though. When it comes to preventing water damage and withstanding hurricane-force winds, aluminum is every bit as good as steel! While it’s very lightweight, this flexible material is surprisingly durable, especially when you hire experienced contractors to handle your metal roof installation.

All of this said, there is one downside to aluminum roofing: the price. Roofing costs always vary, but in general, an aluminum roof will cost more than a steel roof. For many property owners, though, this kind of durable, comprehensive protection is well worth the extra investment!
Metal Roof Installation Styles


When it comes to metal roofing, what you put on it isn’t the only important thing. You also need to carefully consider how your new metal roof will be installed. This decision will impact how long your roof lasts as well as how much your metal roof installation costs, so it’s certainly an important one!

Now, it’s time to look at the three most popular options when it comes to installing a new metal roof in Florida!
Exposed Fastener Metal Roofing
If you’re looking for affordable metal roofing, there’s no better option than exposed fasteners. With this type of metal roof, your chosen material is shaped into corrugated metal panels. During your metal roof installation, contractors will drill these panels down directly into your roof. This keeps manufacturing and labor costs low while ensuring that your roof stays put even during a hurricane!

There are downsides to this approach, though. For one thing, it gives a more industrial appearance that some homeowners love, but others find a little off-putting. Notably, you can still paint exposed fastener metal roofs, which can remove some of that industrial aesthetic.

The other issue is with durability. Exposed fastener metal roofs last for about 40 years on average because the metal can’t freely expand and contract with the sun’s heat, which causes premature wear and tear. Additionally, exposed fasteners get worn down by the elements over the years and may need repairs. While 40 years is still a good lifespan, especially compared to shingles, it simply isn’t the best that metal roofing can do.

On the whole, exposed fastener metal roofs are an affordable option that, while not the very best of metal roofing, can still protect your property for decades!
Hidden Fastener Metal Roofing
Metal roofs with hidden fasteners, also called standing seam metal roofs, are the gold standard. These flat roofing panels have a slight ridge at the end of the panel, which is where they attach together. Since these fasteners are located underneath the roofing panel, they’re much better protected.

Better protection means a longer life for your roof. Your hidden fasteners will last much longer than exposed ones, and since your panels aren’t drilled into place, they can expand and contract slightly throughout the day. Additionally, standing seam metal roofs look great on residential structures. This makes them one of the most in-demand roofing materials in Florida!

As you might have guessed, though, standing seam is fairly expensive. It falls solidly into the “luxury” category of roofing materials, meaning you’ll pay quite a bit for a standing seam metal roof installation. Still though, with a lifespan that ranges from 50-70 years, standing seam is well worth the investment for these extra years of protection.
Metal Shingles
Technically speaking, metal shingles also have exposed fasteners. This means that they’re drilled into your roof. But unlike conventional exposed fastener roofing systems, metal shingles are coated in a layer of protective stone granules. While this doesn’t change the downsides of having exposed fasteners, it does come with some important perks.

For one thing, metal shingles look a lot like shingle roofs. This gives them a much more classic, welcoming aesthetic. Additionally, the granules help protect against denting. This is a big help in Florida, where storm debris and hail can do superficial damage to your metal roof!

And in terms of cost, steel shingles represent a middle ground between exposed fastener roofs and standing seam. All in all, metal shingles are a great option for your metal roof installation if you want the protection of metal and the familiar look of shingles.

As your local roofing partner, we’ll be happy to either prepare a single estimate for your chosen material and style or prepare multiple estimates to help you compare your options!

### How Much Does Soffit Replacement Cost in Florida?

Shingles get the limelight, but your soffits and fascia do essential work to protect your home. This includes providing ventilation as well as protecting your roof from water damage. So when you have damaged soffits, it’s important to act quickly to restore your roof’s protection. But how much does soffit replacement cost?

We’re here to answer exactly that question. We’re PITCH Roofing, and as a full-service roofing company, we know all about soffit repair costs in Florida. Today, we’re covering everything you need to know about soffits and how much your repairs could cost you!
What Are Soffits and Fascia?


Before we dive into soffit replacement costs, it’s important to be clear on what soffits are. Soffits and fascia are located beneath your roof’s overhang. From this position, they can help vent out hot air and prevent rain from being blown into your attic during a storm.

Fascia is the vertical board that you find beneath your roof’s overhang. Beneath this board is usually where you’ll find vents to keep your attic cool and dry. Beneath this is a horizontal board, which makes up your soffits. In addition to preventing water damage, your soffits also keep out pests! This makes them absolutely essential in Florida, where roofing pests can cause a whole host of headaches.

Damage to either of these boards will require immediate repairs by licensed contractors in your neighborhood. But how much will those repairs run you? Let’s discuss soffit and fascia repair costs in Florida!
Soffit Replacement Cost Factors
To start, we can confidently say that the average soffit replacement costs around $2,500. That doesn’t mean you’re going to pay anything near that cost, though. While that is the average cost, there are plenty of unique factors that could determine how much you actually end up paying for soffit repairs.

To help you get a better idea of what your soffit replacement costs will be, let’s talk about these factors and how they’ll influence your total roofing costs!
1. How Much Soffit You’re Replacing
Depending on the extent of the damage to your soffits, you may need larger or smaller repairs. For example, paint peeling on one small part of your soffits is a good reason to call a professional, but it’s not indicative of a major issue. This means you’ll likely end up with lower soffit replacement costs.

If you have rot throughout a large section of your soffits, though, you’re looking at a much larger repair job. Not only will it take more labor to replace your soffits, but you’ll also pay more for the extra materials needed to replace the damaged sections. For jobs like these, you could end up paying more than the average cost for soffit repairs.
2. Your Soffit Materials
Some homeowners are surprised to learn that soffits and fascia come in a variety of material options. Each one has its own pros and cons, and which material you choose will profoundly affect your soffit replacement costs. Let’s look at some of your most common soffit material options in Florida:

 	Wood: The great thing about wood soffits is that they’re very affordable. They do tend to age faster than other materials, though, due to rot from Florida’s year-round humidity. One way to prevent this kind of damage is by painting them, which can extend the life of your soffits and fascia.

 	Vinyl: Vinyl represents a middle ground between wood and aluminum. It’s not as expensive as vinyl, but it’s considerably more durable than wood soffits, which can help lower your roofing costs by preventing future repairs!

You probably aren’t shocked to hear that which roofers you pick will impact how much you pay in soffit replacement costs. In reality, a lot of your labor costs will come down to your contractor’s overhead — costs like office space, crews, customer service professionals, etc. Every roofer has to pay these costs, but some pay more than others. ### What Is a Low-Slope Roof? Flat Roofing Material Options & Costs

Whether you’re getting a new roof for a residential or commercial property, it’s normal to find the jargon a little confusing. This can make roof replacement more difficult, especially when you have a low-slope roof. While there are many types of roofs in Florida, low-slope roofs have unique concerns that need addressing.

We’re here to answer your questions and eliminate any confusion about low-slope roofing! PITCH Roofing is a local roofing company that’s owned and operated by experienced Florida roofers. Join us today as we answer all of your questions about low-slope roofing and how to get the best new roof for your property!
What Is a Low-Slope Roof?


In order to understand what a low-slope roof is, we first have to talk about pitch. Your roof’s pitch is essentially the angle of its steepness. When discussing different roof pitches, the first number reflects the number of inches (or feet) it rises vertically per the second number, the number of inches (or feet) it extends horizontally.

In Florida, the average pitch of a roof runs from 4:12 to 9:12. Shingles are the most popular roofing materials for these structures since water runs freely off the roof without much risk of pooling. With a low-slope roof, though, the situation is very different.

A low-slope roof is any roof with a pitch below 2:12. While the difference between a pitch of 2:12 and 4:12 may not sound like much, we can say with certainty that it completely changes the needs of your roof. Because low-slope roofs are much less steep, they run into roofing problems that normal-slope roofs don’t.

To give you an idea of what problems your low-slope roof will have to avoid, let’s talk about the common pitfalls of low-slope roofs!
Low-Slope Roofing Problems
You may have heard of low-slope roofing referred to as flat roofing before. While low-slope roofs aren’t actually flat, they’re close enough that the name has caught on in popularity. And given the types of issues that these roofs run into, it can be helpful to imagine them as being more or less flat.

For many low-slope roofs, the primary issue they run into is water ponding. Because they’re not steep, these roofs can struggle to move water off your roof. According to the latest Florida building codes, low-slope roofs need to be installed with a minimum slope of one-fourth of a vertical inch for every 12 horizontal inches. In theory, this is enough to keep your roof draining and prevent ponding.

In practice, though, things can be a little more complicated. Installation errors, storm debris, or normal wear and tear can all create problems with water draining from your roof. This leads to puddles forming on your roof, which not even asphalt shingles can keep out.

That’s why flat roofs don’t use asphalt shingles. Instead, they have specialized low-slope roofing materials that prevent water from penetrating your roofing system. You’ll need to pick a flat roofing material when replacing your roof, so let’s talk about your best options for protection in Florida!
Flat Roofing Materials in Florida


While a low-slope roof has unique concerns, there are great options to protect your roof. As experienced Florida roofers, we tend to recommend two distinct options. They each have their pros and cons, so it’s important to be fully informed before making a decision!
Modified Bitumen Roofing
Similar to shingles, modified bitumen is also made using asphalt. However, the asphalt in mod bit roofing is rubberized to make it more flexible and better suited to low-slope roofs. The result is a flat roofing system that can expand and contract with the sun’s heat while staying water-resistant enough to keep out standing water.

That’s why modified bitumen has been a staple for low-slope roofs for over 50 years. These durable, hardy roofs can resist puncture damage as well as the sun’s UV rays, which are two big problems for flat roofs in Florida. In fact, the protection is so good that modified bitumen roofs last for 20 years on average!

The best part may be the price, though. Modified bitumen is the most affordable low-slope roofing material in Florida. On average, mod bit roofs cost between $4 and $8 per square foot in Florida, which makes them very popular among Floridians looking for the most affordable roof.
TPO Roofing
TPO, or thermoplastic polyolefin, is a more modern roofing material. This material came to the roofing market in the 90s and has exploded in popularity ever since. As a single-ply roofing membrane, roofers install TPO as a single layer across your roof. Despite being only one layer, though, TPO can do a great job protecting your low-slope roof.

Because it’s a rubber roof, TPO resists water damage even better than modified bitumen. While no roof can be considered 100% waterproof, TPO certainly comes close. There are downsides, though. TPO roofs only have one layer, which means they’re more vulnerable to puncture damage from storm debris or hail. Additionally, the sun can wear down your roof’s seams over time, which can shorten the life of your roof.

Even with these issues, though, TPO roofs still hold up well. Nobody is sure exactly how long TPO roofs last because they’re so new on the market, but general estimates range from 20 to 30 years. This is a great deal for the price, which is only slightly higher than that of modified bitumen. In Florida, you can expect to pay $4 to $10 per square foot for a TPO roof. This makes them a budget-friendly option for your low-slope roof replacement!
Get a Free Low-Slope Roofing Estimate

For your free, no-obligation estimate, call us at (727) 677-4824 or schedule your estimate online. ### Modified Bitumen vs. TPO Roofing in Florida

Did you know that Florida has more flat roofs than average? In many parts of the US, flat roofs are only really seen on commercial structures. However, here in the Sunshine State, many homes also feature full or partial flat roofs. Since flat roofs are so common here, both homeowners and commercial property owners are asking: how do I choose between modified bitumen vs. TPO for my new flat roof?

It’s a tough choice, but we’re here to give you the information you need to make it. We’re PITCH Roofing, and as veteran Florida roofers, we’ve replaced more than our fair share of flat roofs in our time. Today, we’re using that know-how to explain your flat roofing options and help you plan your flat roof replacement! Now, let’s start with some background on modified bitumen or TPO.
What Is Modified Bitumen?
Modified bitumen, also called modbit, has been a staple of flat roofing for over 50 years. This flat roofing material is made from durable asphalt, flexible polymerized rubber, and resilient fiberglass. The combination of these three components is a strong flat roofing material that can stand up to the worst of Florida’s weather patterns.

That protection is essential because flat roofs in Florida have a lot of work to do. Between water damage and punctures from storm debris or hail, there are more than a few hazards that your flat roof needs to be able to handle. Thankfully, as a tried and trued flat roofing material, modified bitumen can give you plenty of peace of mind.
What Is TPO Roofing?
TPO is short for thermoplastic polyolefin, but what does that mean, exactly? In short, it means that TPO is a kind of rubberized roofing material. This gives it unparalleled water resistance, which will keep your roof safe and dry through nearly any storm.

TPO roofing is a single-ply membrane that first came to the market in the 1990s. This makes it an exciting new roofing technology that offers the latest in flat roof protection. In many ways, the question of modified bitumen vs. TPO is an issue of choosing the tried and true classic or the latest roofing advancements.
Modified Bitumen vs. TPO for Flat Roofs in Florida


When comparing TPO and modified bitumen, there isn’t an easy answer to which one is best. To make the best decision for your home, you’ll have to compare these roofing materials apples to apples. Let us walk you through how modified bitumen and TPO compare when it comes to durability, longevity, and cost!
Roof Durability
In Florida, flat roofs have plenty of hazards to withstand. In addition to the regular issues of pooling water, our flat roofs also need to withstand extreme UV exposure and impact damage. This is a tall order, so does modified bitumen or TPO deliver better results?

Well, it depends. When it comes to water resistance, nothing beats TPO roofing. Because of its polymerized rubber and plastic, it holds up well even to standing water. In theory, there should never be standing water on your roof because it should have a slope that is high enough to drain. If there is an issue with this, though, you’ll be glad you have TPO roofing to keep your roof dry.

For impact damage and UV exposure, though, modified bitumen still offers the best protection. TPO seams can loosen as UV rays break them down, which can shorten your roof’s life. And since TPO is a single-ply roofing material, it’s very vulnerable to impact damage from windborne storm debris.

So which one is more durable, modified bitumen or TPO? We may have to call this one a tie. While TPO roofing has the better water resistance of the two, modified bitumen stands up to storm debris and UV rays like no other.
Roof Longevity
When you’re paying for a flat roof, you want it to last for a long time. So when comparing modified bitumen vs. TPO, we’re of course going to talk about which roofing material lasts longer. And while these flat roofs were evenly matched in durability, there is a clear winner for longevity.

Modified bitumen roofing lasts for around 20 years on average. This makes sense — asphalt shingles have a similar material composition and last for about as long. As a newer bit of roofing technology, though, TPO can beat this number. TPO roofing lasts for 20-30 years on average, so while it’s not a guarantee that your TPO roof will last longer than modified bitumen, there is a very strong possibility.

Whether your TPO roof lasts 20 or 30 years will depend on how long you take care of it. Remember those durability issues we pointed out before? Keeping up on your roof inspections and repairs is the best way to make sure that those issues don’t lead to premature failure of your TPO roof.
Flat Roofing Costs


Finally, everyone wants to know how much their new roof will cost. This can be tricky to figure out, though. After all, roofing costs depend on the size of your roof, its unique features, location, and even which contractors you choose. While we can’t tell you exactly how much your new roof will cost without preparing a personalized quote, we can tell you whether modified bitumen or TPO is more affordable.

Modified bitumen flat roofing costs between $4 and $8 per square foot, making it one of the most affordable options for flat roofing in Florida. Between modified bitumen and TPO, this is definitely the more affordable choice. But it’s not a night and day difference. TPO roofing costs $5 to $10 per square foot, so the prices are comparable.

Ultimately, we don’t recommend letting price be the only factor influencing your decision. While we understand that everyone wants the lowest flat roofing costs possible, it’s important to consider what kind of protection you’re getting for your investment. Flat roofs need to protect your home or commercial property for decades, so it only makes sense to choose the material that you think will best protect your property.

### What Is the Average Cost to Tear Off and Replace a Roof?

Sooner or later, every roof needs replacing. And whether you’re replacing a roof due to old age or bad luck with the latest hurricane, it’s natural to worry about your roof replacement costs. But what’s the average cost to tear off and replace a roof in Florida?

Well, that depends on what you mean by “average.” Don’t worry though — PITCH Roofing is here to answer all of your questions about the cost of tearing off your old roof and installing a new one. Stick with us as we give you a comprehensive guide to roofing prices in Florida!
The Average Cost to Tear Off and Replace a Roof in Florida


 

If you really want the average cost to tear off and replace a roof in Florida, we could say that the average cost of a new roof is between $9,000 and $16,000 in the Sunshine State. But that doesn’t necessarily mean that that’s what you’re going to pay for your new roof.

Your roof replacement costs are way too complicated to just go with the average cost. Roof replacement costs are determined by the size of your roof, its pitch, and any unique roofing features like skylights or chimneys.

But more than just that, your roofing materials have a profound impact on how much you’ll pay for a roof in Florida. That’s why we’re going to look at the material costs for different types of roofing. By comparing them side by side, you’ll be able to get a much better idea of how much your new roof will actually cost!
Asphalt Shingle Roofing Costs
Of all the roofing materials, asphalt shingle roofing costs are the closest to Florida’s state average. Why? Because they’re the most popular roofing material. Made with a fiberglass baseboard that’s then covered in a thick layer of asphalt and topped with stone granules, these shingles last for 20 to 25 years and are durable enough to stand up to hurricane-force winds.

Another reason for shingles’ popularity is their low manufacturing costs. When buying high-quality architectural shingles, expect to pay between $5 and $9 per square foot. Since the average house in Florida has a roof of roughly 1,700 square feet, your average cost to tear off and replace a shingle roof would be between $8,500 and $15,3000.
Tile Roof Replacement Costs
Florida was one of the first places in North America to receive tile roofing, and it’s been a part of Florida living ever since. Generally considered a higher-end roofing material, tile roofs usually come with two material options: clay or concrete. Regardless of which option you pick, you can expect a lot of style options and great, long-lasting durability.

Concrete tiles are good for 50 years of protection, and they’re all but unbeatable when it comes to wind resistance. That makes them perfect for hurricane season, but how much do they cost? On average, concrete tile roofing costs between $9 and $19 per square foot. So the average cost to tear off and replace a roof with clay tiles would be between $15,300 and $32,3000.

Clay roofing tiles have a minimum lifespan similar to that of concrete tiles, about 50 years, but they can last up to a century or more with proper maintenance. These extra years of protection come at a premium, though. As a luxury roofing material, clay tile roofs cost between $12 and $21 per square foot. This puts your average clay tile roof replacement costs at anywhere from $20,400 to $35,700.
Metal Roofing Prices


Of all the roofing materials in Florida, metal roofing is one of the most difficult to find an average cost for. That’s because the average cost of a metal roof replacement depends on which type of metal roofing you’re talking about. And in addition to different types of metal, metal roofs also come with a variety of fastener options that make all the difference in the durability and cost of your new roof.

To give you an idea of the average cost to tear off and replace a metal roof, let’s start with exposed fastener metal roofing. Made with corrugated metal roofing sheets that contractors drill down onto your roof, this type of metal roofing is by far the most affordable. Exposed fastener metal roofing costs $7 to $12 per square foot. On the average 1,700-square-foot roof, that means paying $11,900 to $20,400 for a new metal roof. Not bad for 30 years of hardy protection!

The opposite of exposed fastener metal roofing is hidden fastener metal roofing, or standing seam. This uses mostly flat roofing sheets that adhere together under the panel, which helps protect your roof. Because of this extra protection, these metal roofs can last for 40-70 years. However, they also cost more to manufacture and install. Standing seam metal roofing costs $10 to $35 per square foot, or $17,000 to $35,000 for a metal roof replacement.

Finally, stone-coated steel roofing provides all the protection of steel roofing with the look of asphalt shingles. By taking metal roofing sheets and coating them in stone granules, manufacturers create metal shingles that look warm and welcoming and can last just as long as standing seam roofing. Thankfully though, it’s much more affordable. Metal shingles cost $7 to $15 per square foot, so $11,900 to $25,500 for a full roof removal and replacement.

### How Long Does a Roof Last? Your Florida Roof Life Expectancy

2024’s hurricane season has been one of the toughest on record. As people repair their roofs and invest in new ones, many homeowners want a roofing system that can withstand Florida’s harshest storms and keep their homes protected for years to come. This begs the question, though, how long does a roof last in Florida?

There is no one-size-fits-all answer, but we can definitely tell you how long you should expect your new roof to last in the Sunshine State. We’re PITCH Roofing, your local roofing partners. As veteran local contractors, we know Central Florida roofing better than anyone. Stick with us as we walk you through how long you can expect your new roof to last!
How Long Does a Roof Last? Material Options Explained


If you want a quick answer, we can say that the average roof in Florida lasts for 20-25 years. If you want an accurate answer, though, then the situation is a little more complicated.

Several different elements will determine how long your roof lasts. These include how well you take care of your roof, your location, and other unique roofing factors. The biggest determiner, though, is the roofing material you choose. Picking your roofing material can make the difference between a 20-year roof and a 70-year roof!

With that in mind, let’s look at how long different roofing materials last in Florida!
Asphalt Shingles
When we said that the average Florida roof lasts for 20-25 years, that was true. But that’s only true because the average Florida roof uses asphalt shingles. Made from fiberglass baseboard, a thick asphalt coating, and protective stone granules, shingles have been the most popular roofing material for decades thanks to their low roofing costs.

As we’ve mentioned, shingles last for about 25 years in Florida. This is a long time for people, but a relatively short time for roofs. While shingles are a great, affordable roofing option, there are certainly better options if you want a longer-lasting roof!
Roofing Tiles
Tiles have been a popular roofing material in Florida for centuries. Traditionally they’re made from hardened clay, but manufacturers also make them with concrete. With either material, you can enjoy a variety of style and color options, including barrel tiles and flat tiles.

There is a noticeable difference in longevity, though. Concrete roofing tiles last for about 50 years on average, whereas clay roofing tiles can last anywhere from 50 to 100 years or more. Clay roofing tiles are some of the longest-lasting roofing materials on the market, so they’re great if you’re committed to investing in longevity!
Metal Roofing
Metal roofs have exploded in popularity across Florida in recent years. They’re one of the best roofing materials for resisting hurricanes, with wind resistance that can withstand even Florida’s major storms. But how long does a metal roof last in Florida?

Well, that depends on the metal roof. Metal roofs come in many different materials, but just as importantly, they also come in a variety of shapes and fastener methods. How long you can expect your metal roof to last will depend on how it’s adhered to your roof:

 	Exposed Fastener Metal Roofs: Because their fasteners are exposed to the elements, these roofs don’t last as long as other metal roofing options. On average, corrugated metal roofing like this lasts for about 30 years.
 	Hidden Fastener Metal Roofs: Also called standing seam metal roofing, these roofs last much longer because the fasteners are safely hidden under the metal panels. That’s why these roofs last 50-70 years!
 	Metal Shingle Roofs: Metal shingles combine the great protection of metal with the classic look of asphalt shingles. On average, metal shingle roofs last for around 50 years in Florida.

How to Tell When You Need a New Roof


In addition to knowing how long a roof lasts, many homeowners also worry about signs that their roof needs to be replaced ASAP. And that’s a valid concern; putting off essential roof replacements can do serious structural damage to your home or commercial property. So how do you know if it’s time to get a new roof?

Some of the common signs you need a roof replacement include:

 	Recurring Leaks: One roof leak is not a sign of serious roofing damage. But if you find yourself with new roof leaks only a few months after fixing your last one, it could mean that there is serious damage to your roof that only replacing can address.
 	Granules in the Gutters: As roofing shingles age, they start to shed that protective coating of stone granules. If you find these in your gutters or at the base of your downspouts, it means that your shingles are reaching the end of their lifespan.
 	Neighbors Getting New Roofs: Many communities are built at the same time. This means that, often, their roofs need replacing at the same time too. If you see several of your neighbors getting new roofs installed, it could mean that it’s time to replace your roof.
 	Age: Roofers can address any individual problem, but they can’t fix age. If your roof is having problems and is at the end of its lifespan, you need a new roof ASAP. It can be tempting to put off a roof replacement, but when the next big storm blows into town, you’ll be glad to have strong, resilient protection.

When it’s time to replace a roof, there’s no way around it. While we understand that roof replacements don’t always come at a convenient time, you have roof financing options available that can help you pay for a new roof without waiting and risking the safety of your property.
