### Clay vs. Concrete Roofing Tiles: An Apples to Apples Comparison

Tile roofing has been a part of life in Florida for centuries — since even before the founding of our nation. While tile roofing has remained a constant, new advances in roofing technology have expanded homeowners’ options when it comes to roof replacements. Specifically, many homeowners are now choosing between clay vs. concrete roofing tiles.

Since it’s not as simple as saying one material is better than the other, we’ll have to do a deep dive to determine which tile roofing material is right for your home. We’re PITCH Roofing, and we’re your local tile roofing experts. Stick with us as we show the good and the bad of clay and concrete roofing tiles!
Comparing Clay vs. Concrete Roofing Tiles in Florida


Every roofing material has its ups and downs, and roofing tiles are no different. To help you decide between clay vs. concrete roofing tiles, we’re looking at these materials side-by-side with regard to costs, longevity, durability, and all the other areas that you want to know about as a homeowner.

Now, let’s get started and see which roofing material is right for you!
Longevity
Everyone wants a roof that will last a long time. Classic asphalt shingles offer about 25 years of life, but homeowners investing in tile roofing expect a little more bang for their buck. Thankfully, both clay and concrete roofing tiles deliver long-lasting roof protection.

Concrete roofing tiles are the shorter-lived of the two, with lifespans averaging about 50 years. Clay tiles, on the other hand, are the longest-lasting roofing material on the market. These natural tiles can last for up to 100 years with proper maintenance and occasional repairs. Both roofing materials will last a long time, but there is simply no beating the longevity of clay tile roofing!
Wind Resistance
When it comes to roofing in Florida, it’s only natural to worry about how your roof will stand up against a hurricane. There is good news, though. Both clay and concrete roofing tiles are more than capable of standing up to even major hurricanes!

For one thing, both tile options are highly wind-resistant. Clay roofing tiles have been found to resist winds up to 150 mph, which is enough to withstand most major hurricanes. Because of their additional weight, concrete tiles boast even better wind resistance, around 180 mph. In both cases, tiles far out-perform asphalt shingles, which have max wind resistances around 130 mph.
Water Resistance
In general, roofing tiles do a great job moving water off your roof and toward your gutters. With tiles, the main concern is preventing water from penetrating into the tile. If this happens, it can cause mold, rot, and a general weakening of your roof’s protection.

When comparing clay vs. concrete roofing tiles, there is a clear winner in this arena. Concrete roofing tiles have a water absorption rate of around 13%. This is more than double the water retention rate of clay tiles, which is closer to 6%. Because of the additional water absorption, concrete tiles more often have problems with mildew, staining, and mold growth.
Impact Resistance


In Florida, there are two main reasons to worry about impact resistance: hail and storm debris. Whether it’s the occasional hail storm or debris whipped up by the high winds of a hurricane, you want your roof to be able to withstand these blows without taking damage. In this arena, one tile roofing material definitely outperforms the other.

While clay tiles have unmatched lifespans, they can also be brittle. Especially in the winter months, any blow to your tiles could shatter them. The good news is that replacing these tiles is a quick and simple repair. However, if you’d rather avoid the headache entirely, concrete roofing tiles are much less likely to crack from hail or storm debris.
Color Fading
Both clay and concrete roofing tiles come in a variety of colors. They acquire these colors in very different ways, though. Clay roofing tiles are naturally colored from their base materials. Concrete roofing tiles, on the other hand, are painted.

While the results look the same on a newly installed roof, they age very differently. As water and UV rays wear on concrete tiles, the paint often starts to lighten and fade. With clay tiles, their color is a natural part of their clay material, so it isn’t bleached by the sun or other elements. This means that clay tiles stay looking their best for longer than concrete tiles!
Weight
Roofing tiles are heavy across the board. That’s part of what makes them so excellent at resisting Florida’s high winds! When a roof is too heavy, though, it can cause issues. These problems can be avoided by installing additional supports, but this can contribute to higher roof replacement costs.

Remember how we said the additional weight of concrete tiles makes them better at resisting wind? Well, it also makes them more likely to require additional structural support before your roof installation. In fact, concrete tiles weigh roughly 40% more than clay tiles, so we’re talking about a major difference that you’ll need to carefully consider when deciding on your new roof.
Roof Replacement Costs
Finally, the big question that every homeowner wants an answer to: how much is my tile roof going to cost? Roofing costs are always highly personalized things, dependent on many unique factors like your roofers, your location, and the specific details of your roof. That said, we can definitively say that when it comes to clay vs. concrete roofing tiles, one option is much more affordable than the other.

Clay roofing tiles cost between $12 and $21 per square foot in Florida. This puts it firmly in the category of luxury roofing materials. Concrete tiles are slightly cheaper with prices ranging from $9 to $19 per square foot. While neither of these materials is cheap, concrete stands out as the more affordable tile roofing option.

### Flat Roofing Tile Costs and Features

Tile roofing has deep roots in Florida. For centuries, the local roofing scene has been dominated by Spanish roofing tiles and other types of barrel tile roofs. To make a change, though, more and more homeowners are turning to flat roofing tiles for a unique roof that stands out in the best way.

We’re PITCH Roofing, and as veteran Florida roofers, we know a thing or two about tile roofing in Florida. Today, we’re talking about flat roofing tiles and how much they cost, your material options, and the unique draws of these unconventional tiles. If you’re interested in getting a bold new tile roof, this could be the perfect roofing material for you!
What Are Flat Roofing Tiles?


Flat roofing tiles come in a variety of colors and materials. The thing that sets them apart, however, is their unique, flat profile. This is different from barrel tiles, which are curved like a barrel cut in half. Flat tiles have no such curves, but they still move water quickly and efficiently off of your roof.

Take, for example, French roofing tiles. These are a kind of flat tile, but they have a unique design feature: two flutes engraved in the middle of the tile. These create two streams for water to use when traveling down your roof. By keeping the water moving, these tiles prevent it from reaching your underlayment, which keeps your roof dry and protected for longer.

In terms of performance, flat roofing tiles perform just as well as barrel tile roofs. In fact, the main deciding factor in how well your tile roof will perform is the material your tiles are made from. To help you plan your tile roof replacement, let’s look at these options a little more in-depth!
Tile Roofing Material Options
When it comes to flat roofing tiles, you have two main options when it comes to materials: concrete and clay. Each of these roofing materials comes with its own ups and downs, so let’s compare them side by side to help you pick the right roofing material for your home.

Concrete tiles are beloved as a more affordable tile roofing material. Despite their lower manufacturing and installation costs, concrete tiles still last for 50 years — much longer than the 25-year lifespan of a shingle roof. They’re also hardy enough to withstand Florida’s hurricanes, with wind resistance as high as 180 mph. If concrete tiles have one downside, it’s that UV rays can bleach their paint and fade their colors, which can require occasional re-painting.

Clay tiles are much more pricey — in fact, they’re so expensive that they’re a luxury roofing material. You can at least be confident that you’re paying for quality, though. Clay flat roofing tiles can last for over 100 years with good tile roof maintenance, and they’re every bit as durable as concrete. They have a leg up on concrete roofing tiles when it comes to aesthetics, too, since their natural color isn’t usually bleached by the sun.

Since material types are the biggest predictor of performance, there isn’t much of a difference in flat roofing tiles vs. barrel tiles when it comes to protecting your home. So why choose flat roofing tiles over Spanish or other barrel roofing tiles?
Why Homeowners Choose Flat Roofing Tiles
Since flat roofing tiles perform about as well as barrel tiles do, it can be confusing to see what all the hubbub is about. But it’s important to remember that a lot of the appeal of tile roofing is the unique, distinctive aesthetic. And it’s safe to say that the looks of barrel roofing tiles are very different from the style of flat tiles.

In Florida, we’ve grown accustomed to the ridged pattern of curved roofing tiles. For many homeowners, this is a classic, timeless look that they love to see replicated on their homes. This is especially popular among homeowners with stucco siding and other Spanish touches to their property.

However, flat tiles offer a chance to buck this trend. Flat tiles come with a specific kind of European charm that looks striking compared to classic Florida roofs. Homeowners often choose flat roofing tiles to have a more unique roof that compliments their individual tastes and aesthetics.

At this point, you know a good deal about flat tiles. There is still one important area to cover, though. How much do flat roofing tiles cost?
The Cost of Flat Roofing Tiles in Florida


Calculating roofing costs is always difficult. Factors like materials, manufacturer, location, and your chosen roofing company will always have a big impact on total costs. And this is even harder to puzzle out with tiles since the style of your tile roof will also impact roof replacement costs.

In general, flat tiles cost less than barrel tiles because they’re lighter weight and thus easier to install. Even with this cost reduction, though, the biggest factor in your roofing costs will be what material your flat roofing tiles are made from.

On average, concrete roofing tiles cost between $9 and $19 per square foot. This is far from cheap, but it’s certainly more affordable than clay. In Florida, you can expect to pay $12 to $21 per square foot for clay roofing tiles.

So how much will you pay for your flat roofing tiles? That number is going to depend on a lot of highly individualized factors. That doesn’t mean you have to go in blind, though. It just means that it’s time to start collecting tile roofing quotes!

### Mobile Home Roofing Costs and Asphalt Shingle Options

Florida weather is infamously harsh on roofs, and 2024 has seen one of the state’s most active hurricane seasons in history. But our weather patterns are especially hard on mobile homes. This makes it all the more crucial that you get quality services when it comes to roofing for trailer homes.

We’re PITCH Roofing, and as your local roofing experts, we’re here to give you the complete rundown on trailer home roofing. That includes calculating the cost of a mobile home roof replacement, your warranty information, and your material options. Keep reading to prepare for your roof replacement!
Roofing Materials for Trailer Homes


When it comes to mobile home roofing materials, asphalt shingles are the gold standard. They’re affordable, durable, and readily available no matter where you are. Even when you stick with asphalt shingles, though, you still have options to consider when the time comes for your roof replacement.
3-Tab Shingles
For a long time, 3-tab shingles were the most popular roofing material in North America. Made using asphalt, fiberglass, and stone granules, these shingles are cheap to produce and easy to install. The simplicity of their design isn’t all positive, though.

The biggest issue with 3-tab shingles is that they don’t last for very long. In the best-case scenario, you’re not likely to get more than 15 years out of a 3-tab shingle roof in Florida. In the worst-case scenario, any storm with winds over 70 mph could seriously damage your 3-tab shingles.

For people who need the cheapest possible roof, though, 3-tab shingles are a solid option. In most cases, however, we recommend choosing roof financing over a low-quality roofing material. Nobody wants another monthly bill, but when it comes to roofing for trailer homes, it’s often better to have the best protection possible.
Architectural Shingles
The roofing scene changed drastically when architectural (dimensional) shingles hit the market in the 1970s. These are also asphalt shingles and they’re made using the same combination of materials as 3-tab shingles. What makes them different, however, is that they’re twice as thick as 3-tab shingles with more layers, which gives the shingle increased heft and weight.

You’d be surprised what a big difference that makes in roofing for trailer homes. Architectural shingles last 20-25 years on average, even in hurricane-prone Florida. This is in part thanks to their improved wind resistance, which allows them to withstand winds up to 130 mph. The added thickness also improves their water resistance and ability to resist rot!

It’s true that architectural shingles are a bit more expensive than 3-tab shingles. But for the increased longevity of your roof, we think they’re well worth the small price increase.
Roofing Warranties for Mobile Homes


When you’re getting a trailer home roof replacement, it’s important to make sure you’re getting high-quality warranties. This is part of why it’s important to carefully choose your roofers. Some roofers are able to offer much stronger warranties than others, and there are some simple ways to tell when you’ve found good contractors with great warranties.

For one thing, you want to have both material and workmanship warranties. In simple terms, material warranties cover roofing problems caused by defective materials — so if your shingles were damaged due to a flaw in the manufacturing, the manufacturer would have to pay to have them replaced.

Workmanship warranties, on the other hand, apply to the work done by contractors on your roof. For example, if your shingles were incorrectly installed, a workmanship warranty guarantees that your roofers have to cover the costs of fixing your roof installation. Keep in mind that for both of these warranties, acts of God are not covered. This means that if a hurricane tears your roof off your home, you will not have coverage because nobody can guarantee protection against a hurricane.

For all other scenarios, though, having strong warranties is a big help. When picking roofing contractors for trailer homes, look for special accreditations. For example, PITCH is a proud Owens Roofing Preferred Contractor. This means we can offer the strongest warranties on both materials and workmanship. Even better, our workmanship warranties are backed by Owens Corning themselves. So even if PITCH wasn’t around by the time you needed roofing help, your warranties would still be backed by Owens Corning!

3-tab shingles cost between $3 and $6 per square foot. This reflects how quick and easy these are to manufacture and install. Since dimensional shingles are thicker and require more raw materials, architectural shingles cost $5 to $9 per square foot.

### Cost of Metal Shingles: Are They Worth the Investment in Florida?

For decades, asphalt shingles have been the go-to roofing material across North America. But as a Florida homeowner, you have unique needs. How Are Metal Shingles Made?


In theory, the concept of a metal shingle is pretty simple: it’s metal made to look like a shingle. But the truth of the matter is more complicated, and the way that manufacturers achieve this distinctive look is going to have a major impact on your roof’s protection.

Metal shingles are made of steel roofing sheets that have been shaped to mimic the look of shingles. Even perfectly sculpted steel can’t replicate the look and texture of asphalt shingles, though. So how do metal shingles end up looking so similar to classic asphalt shingles?

Manufacturers achieve this look through a process that adheres stone granules across the length of the metal roofing sheets. This replicates how real asphalt shingles are made since shingle manufacturers coat asphalt in stone granules to provide protection against storm debris and UV rays. By mimicking the process, manufacturers give metal shingles the same protective benefits and look!

This explains how stone-coated steel roofing is made, but it doesn’t cover the cost of metal shingles or why they’re so quickly gaining popularity in Florida. For that, we’ll have to continue our deep dive into metal shingle roofing in Florida!
Metal Shingle Roofing Features

Long Lifespans
When you get a new roof, you want it to last for a long time. That’s exactly what these roofing materials provide — metal shingles last for 50 years on average. Compare that to the 20-25-year lifespan of asphalt shingles, and it’s no wonder why the higher cost of metal shingles hasn’t stopped people from making the switch to this superior roofing material.
Hurricane Resistant
Standing up to a hurricane is a tall order for any roof, but metal shingles are up to the task. These shingles resist UV damage, water damage, and even denting. The best part, though? Metal shingles resist winds up to 170 mph. When you invest in a metal shingle roof, you can be confident that it’s not going anywhere anytime soon.
Color Versatility
Part of the appeal of asphalt shingles has always been the ability to get the exact right color for your roof. This is just another way that metal shingles offer all of the advantages of asphalt shingles without the drawbacks. Metal shingles come in a wide variety of colors, so you’ll be able to get the exact aesthetic that you want without skimping on protection for your property.
Energy Efficiency
Like many types of metal roofing, metal shingles are extremely energy efficient. Since they help reflect UV rays away from your home, they keep things cooler and make it so your AC system doesn’t have to work as hard. This is definitely a factor that you should consider when calculating the total cost of metal shingles!

### Tile Roof Maintenance

Florida’s love of tile roofing goes all the way back to some of the first Spanish colonies in North America. While our love of tile roofing has stayed, we’ve found new ways to make tile roofs last longer and provide better home protection. Thanks to these new tile roof maintenance strategies, tile roofs are better than ever!

If you’re not sure how to take care of your roof, then let us give you the most up-to-date tips on tile roof maintenance. We’re PITCH Roofing and as veteran Florida contractors, it’s our pleasure to keep you current on the best ways to take care of your roof so you can get the most value out of your investment in your home. Keep reading for all the dos and dont’s of maintaining a tile roof in Florida!
Tile Roof Maintenance Don’ts


You know that old saying, “an ounce of prevention is worth more than a pound of cure”? That holds true with tile roof maintenance, too. That’s why we’re starting with the things you should avoid doing to make sure your tile roof has a long, healthy life!
Don’t: Get on Your Tile Roof
As a homeowner, sometimes you may want to access your roof, whether you’re inspecting for damage or trying to do some minor repairs. This isn’t a big deal when you have asphalt shingles, since these are fairly resistant to occasional foot traffic. Tile roofs are a different story, though.

Roofing tiles are not built to support the weight of an adult human. In fact, clay tiles are fairly brittle, so any substantial amount of weight runs the risk of cracking the tile and damaging your roof further.

There are ways to safely navigate tile roofs, but they require specialized equipment and know-how. If you need to have tile roof maintenance conducted on your home, it’s best to leave any accessing of your roof to licensed professionals who know how to fix issues on your roof without accidentally crushing a tile and causing new problems.
Don’t: Overlook Cracks in Your Tiles
As we mentioned, tiles are often brittle. This means that anything from hail to storm debris has a chance of damaging your tiles. As roofers, one of the biggest tile roof maintenance failures that we see is homeowners not acting quickly when there is a problem like this on their roofs.

Even if the crack in your tile seems minor, it’s still important to get roof repairs ASAP. Over time, damage has a tendency to spread — for example, maybe the crack slowly lets water accumulate under your tiles and degrade your underlayment. If this happens, you’ve gone from a quick and easy fix to replacing a section of your roof.

We understand that it’s hard to know for sure when a roofing problem is serious. But one rule of tile roof maintenance is that if you suspect that there’s a problem, it’s worth it to have a roofer come out and take a look just to be sure. You spent a lot of money on your tile roof, so don’t endanger that investment by ignoring signs of wear and tear!
Don’t: Pressure Wash Your Tile Roof
Over time, tile roofs can occasionally develop mold or other kinds of discoloration. This is especially true in humid Florida. While wanting a pristine tile roof is totally normal, we strongly discourage power washing your tile roof to clean it.

There are two main dangers when it comes to power washing your roof. First, the water pressure is likely to crack your tiles. And even if it doesn’t, it will force water beneath your tiles, which can weaken your underlayment and lead to structural concerns for your entire roofing system. Keeping your roof clean is part of good tile roof maintenance, but using a pressure washer is one of the worst things you can do for a Florida tile roof!
Tile Roof Maintenance Dos


Now that we’ve covered the biggest tile roof maintenance mistakes to avoid, it’s time to talk about the maintenance that will keep your tile roof looking and performing its best for decades. Keep reading for our simple and easy tips!
Do: Set Up Regular Roof Inspections
In Florida, roof inspections are a 100% necessary part of tile roof maintenance. While the general wisdom everywhere is to get your roof inspected once a year, especially if your roof is more than five years old, Floridians may need even more regular roof inspections.

In addition to annual roof inspections, you should have a professional look at your roof after any major storm. As we mentioned, storm debris can do a real number on tile roofs, so it’s best to get ahead of any issues and make sure you’re being proactive. While this can seem like an additional expense, this will actually save you money across the lifetime of your roof by keeping any repair costs as low as possible.
Do: Get Professional Cleaning Services
Everyone loves the pristine look of a tile roof. But over time, that beauty will get hidden under layers of algae, mildew, and dirt. Since trying to clean your own tile roof will likely lead to cracked tiles at best and serious accidents at worst, we strongly encourage hiring a professional crew to clean your roof.

Your exact mileage may vary, but generally, we recommend getting a tile roof cleaning every 3 to 5 years. This ensures that any buildup doesn’t have time to set into your tiles, which will keep them from weakening over the life of your roof. We know that nobody wants another tile roof maintenance bill, but this really is a crucial step that protects both the aesthetics and the performance of your roof.
Do: Keep Gutters and Downspouts Clear
Roofing tiles are designed to help move water off your roof. Whether that’s through divots in French tiles or the rounded edge of barrel tiles, these roofing materials are excellent at moving water to the edge of your roof. But when leaves and other debris pile up, they can block the flow of water and lead to trapped water getting into places it shouldn’t.

That’s why you should regularly take a look at your gutters and downspouts to make sure they’re functioning as intended. When your gutters overflow, they can wear away at your home’s foundation. While this isn’t an immediate concern, over time it could do major damage to your home and lead to extremely costly repairs.

The good news about this tile roof maintenance tip is that you probably won’t have to clear leaves and other debris very often. Most professionals recommend cleaning your gutters twice a year, which is a worthy sacrifice for keeping your home protected and safe!

As some of the top-rated roofers in Florida, we’ve mastered tile roof installations, repairs, and inspections. ### Pros and Cons of Metal Tile Roofing in Florida

Tile roofing has been a part of Florida history for centuries, ever since Spanish settlers established their first colonies here. Although concrete and clay tile roofs are still popular roofing materials in Florida, new metal tile roof technology is giving these classic options a run for their money.

But is a metal tile roof worth the investment in Florida? That’s what we’re here to help you figure out. We’re PITCH Roofing, and as veteran Florida roofers, we consider it our responsibility to share up-to-date information on your local roofing options. Stick with us as we cover everything you need to know about metal roofing tiles!
What Is a Metal Tile Roof?


If you’ve heard of stone-coated steel roofs before, then you’ve pretty much got the idea of what a metal tile roof is. These high-quality roofs start with sheets of metal — usually some type of steel, although specifics will depend on your manufacturer. During manufacturing, the metal sheets are sculpted to mimic the look of traditional roofing tiles. The steel is then coated in a protective alloy to prevent rust, which usually includes some combination of zinc and/or aluminum.

From there, manufacturers cover the steel sheet in small stone granules and paint. Each provides another layer of protection against wear and tear. Additionally, the paint helps bind the granules to the steel, ensuring that they don’t go anywhere any time soon.

Once the tiles are finished, the only step left to do is install your metal tile roof. While traditional concrete or clay tiles are installed tile-by-tile, metal tile roofs are faster to install than clay tiles. That’s because they’re installed by the sheet and drilled down directly into your roof.

This covers the basics of what metal roofing tiles are, but are they a good idea for Florida homeowners? To answer that, we have to look at the good and the bad of metal tile roofs.
Pros and Cons of a Metal Tile Roof
While homeowners often have preferences about roofing materials, there is no such thing as a “perfect” roof. Every roof comes with great features in durability or longevity or cost, but every roof also has its downsides. To see if a metal tile roof is the right fit for your home, we have to look at the pros and the cons of this roofing material!
Pro: The Unbeatable Protection of Metal
Clay tile roofs offer great protection. But a metal tile roof has its own protective features to brag about. Some of the biggest advantages to getting a stone-coated steel roof include:

 	Wind resistance up to 170 mph
 	Resistance to water damage and mold development
 	Virtual immunity to pest infestations
 	Rust resistance
 	Class A fire rating

This makes a metal tile roof at least as good at protecting your home as a clay tile roof, if not more so. And when you compare metal tiles to concrete tiles, it’s clear that metal tiles offer much better, more robust protection.
Con: Prone to Denting
Thankfully, most parts of Florida don’t see much hail in a year. But whether it’s the odd hailstorm or storm debris, anything hitting your roof at a high velocity can leave a dent in your metal tiles. This is very rarely a structural concern, but it still creates an aesthetic problem that many homeowners don’t care for.

On the flipside, that same storm debris or hail could shatter a clay tile. This means that while a metal tile roof may need repairs after experiencing impact damage, the issue is at least less serious than with a clay tile roof, since a shattered tile is a much more immediate threat to the safety of your roof.
Pro: All the Versatility of Clay Tile Roofs
 

Part of what Florida homeowners appreciate about tile roofs is the color and style options. Barrel tiles can look very different from flat tiles, and many people prefer a specific look of tile. Thankfully, you don’t have to sacrifice any of this when you choose a metal tile roof.

Metal roofing tiles have the same style options as clay tiles, which means you can get the exact roof you’ve always dreamed of. Additionally, metal tile roofs come in just as many color options as clay or concrete tiles. So whether you prefer neutral tones or the classic red of clay, getting a metal tile roof will not mean sacrificing your aesthetic preferences.

The end result is a roof that is all but indistinguishable from real clay tiles. For homeowners who want the look of clay but the protection of steel, there is no better option on the market!
Con: Color Fading Over Time
Florida is called the Sunshine State for a reason: we get a lot of UV rays all year round. While that’s nice for us residents, it’s not so nice for our roofs. With a metal tile roof, you can expect your tiles to lose some of their color over the lifespan of your roof. That’s because the paint is slowly broken down by UV rays, which can cause bleaching.

This is not a problem for clay tiles, but it has been known to happen with concrete tile roofs, which are painted similarly to metal tiles. And since the paint helps keep the stone granules attached to your steel sheets, it’s important to stay ahead of this issue. If you choose to get a metal tile roof, you’ll want to keep up on maintenance and have your roof re-painted as needed. Your mileage will vary, but this is usually necessary once every 10 to 15 years or so.
Pro: Lower Roofing Costs Than Clay Tile Roofs
It’s rare for metal roofs to not be the expensive option, but in this case, it’s true. While a metal tile roof will be much more expensive than asphalt shingles, it will likely cost less than a clay tile roof replacement. But how much will it cost, exactly?

Unless you’re getting a quote tailored to your roof, there is always some guesswork with roofing costs. But in general, a metal tile roof costs between $7 and $15 per square foot. This is considerably less than the $12 to $21 per square foot cost of clay tile roofs.

This results in a lot of savings for homeowners without sacrificing style or performance. While clay tile roofs can last for up to 100 years in some cases, more often, they last for about 50 years in Florida. This makes them easy to compare to metal tile roofs, which also last for about 50 years before needing replacing. This means that you can expect real savings when you choose a metal tile roof!

And unlike other roofers, the professionals at PITCH make getting a metal tile roof cost estimate quick and easy.

### A Florida Buyer's Guide to Metal Shingle Roofs

For decades, asphalt shingles have been the most popular roofing material in North America. Then, when metal roofing came onto the market, many people saw the enhanced durability and longevity of metal roofing and wanted to make a switch. However, some homeowners don’t like the distinct look of a metal roof. If this sounds like you, then a metal shingle roof can offer you the best of both worlds.

We’re PITCH Roofing, and as your local roofing partner, we know the ins and outs of both shingle and metal roofing. Keep reading for our guide to metal shingles for Florida homeowners, where we’ll answer all your questions about metal shingle makeup, its main features, and how much it costs!
What Is a Metal Shingle Roof?


The main appeal of a metal shingle roof is that it combines the best of shingles and the best of metal roofing. This means you get the warm, familiar appearance of shingles while also enjoying the next-generation protection of metal roofs. But how do they work?

Like with other types of metal roofs, it all starts with a sheet of metal. Usually made from steel coated in a protective alloy, manufacturers then coat the metal sheets in protective stone granules. This is similar to the process with asphalt shingles, which are coated in stone granules to create the familiar shingle look that we all know and love.

Once the metal shingles are finished, the only thing left is for your roofers to install them. This means screwing down the new metal shingles over top of your roof decking and water-resistant underlayment. This is known as the exposed fastener method, and it ensures that your roof won’t be going anywhere anytime soon.

The end result is a roof with the look of asphalt shingles but the unbeatable protection of steel. How does this compare to traditional asphalt shingles, though? Let’s find out by comparing them side by side.
Metal Shingle Roof vs. Asphalt Shingle Roof


In roofing, there are generally three questions that homeowners want answers to. These are:

 	How long will my new roof last?
 	What are my new roof’s safety features?
 	How much will my new roof cost?

To answer all of these questions, we’re going to compare metal shingles and asphalt shingles in each of these areas. Keep reading for answers to all of your questions about metal shingle roofing in Florida!
Longevity
When talking about how long your new roof will last, there is a clear difference between metal shingles and asphalt shingles. For a long time, 3-tab shingles were the industry standard, which only lasted for 15 years at best. With new architectural shingles, though, asphalt shingles can last as long as 20 to 25 years, even with Florida’s extreme weather patterns.

Even with this upgrade, though, asphalt shingles just can’t compete with metal shingles when it comes to roofing lifespans. A metal shingle roof lasts for 50 years on average. This makes their lifespan literally double that of asphalt shingles!

Of course, how long your roof lasts isn’t the only thing you need to think about when planning a roof replacement. You’ll also need to consider how your roof is going to withstand your local weather.
Durability
If you’ve ever taken a walk through a Florida neighborhood after a hurricane, you probably saw more than a few shingles scattered on the ground. That’s because even top-rated asphalt shingles can only withstand winds up to 130 mph. If winds get higher than that, as they easily can during major hurricanes, you can count on losing some shingles, especially if your roof is more than five years old.

This isn’t the only problem that asphalt shingles experience, either. While they’re water-resistant, they can still rot and develop mold thanks to Florida’s high humidity, especially as your roof gets older. For these reasons, occasional roof repairs are an expected part of having asphalt shingles.

Metal shingle roofs are a very different story. These shingles have been tested and found to withstand winds up to 170 mph — well above the 157 mph minimum for a Category 5 hurricane. While no roof can completely guarantee protection against the worst storms, a metal shingle roof is about as close as you can get to foolproof protection.

And thanks to their rust-resistant coatings and protective granules, metal roofs don’t run the same risk of rotting or developing mold that shingle roofs do. This also makes them less attractive to pests, which can sometimes make homes in damaged roofs. On the whole, this means that metal shingles need much fewer repairs than asphalt shingles and are better suited to Florida’s unique environment.

There is one exception, though. Because metal shingles use exposed fasteners sitting on top of your roof, the fasteners can be worn down by the elements over time. This usually looks like rust and other signs of weathering, which is why it’s important to get occasional roof inspections as your metal shingle roof ages. This way, you can get ahead of any potential issues and keep roof repair costs low.
Cost
Finally, the biggest question homeowners have: How much will my roof cost? Calculating roofing costs is a little tricky. This is because the exact figure will always depend on the size and unique features of your roof. But by talking about the average cost per square foot, we can give you a rough idea of how much your new shingle roof will cost.

Asphalt shingle roofs cost between $5 and $9 per square foot. This makes them hands-down the most affordable roofing material on the market. On a 1,700-square-foot home, that looks like $8,500 to $15,300 for your asphalt shingle roof replacement.

There’s no denying that metal shingles are much more expensive. A metal shingle roof averages $7 to $15 per square foot. On that same roof, you’re looking at metal roof replacement costs between $14,000 and $30,000.

It’s important to contextualize these numbers. Asphalt shingles are cheaper, yes, but metal shingles last twice as long. For this reason, it can be wise to look at metal shingles as a long-term investment in your property. Additionally, metal shingles also need fewer repairs than asphalt shingle roofs, so you’ll spend less over the lifetime of your metal shingle roof.

### What Is Roof Decking & How Much Does It Cost?

Whether you’re replacing an old roof or finalizing a new construction, roof decking is an essential part of your roofing system. While other parts of your roofing system, like shingles or metal, get a lot of the focus when it’s time to install a new roof, roof decking is the foundation of any healthy roof.

If you’ve heard of roof decking but aren’t sure what it is or why it’s important, we’ve got you covered. As your local roofing partner, PITCH Roofing is here to answer all of your questions about Florida roofing. Keep reading as we explain decking and how it affects the rest of your structure!
What Is Roof Decking and How Does It Work?


While we often talk about shingle roofs or metal roofs, your roof is much more than just the material on top. There’s a whole system of supports and protections that work together to keep your roof functioning. Your roof decking is the base of this system, a series of wooden boards that the rest of your roof rests on top of.

Since your decking sits under the rest of your roof, it probably won’t have many issues. That doesn’t mean that it’s completely protected, though. Severe leaks that bypass your water-resistant underlayment can damage your decking and may even lead to rot. As you might imagine, any weakening in your decking could put your entire roofing system at risk.

This covers the basics of decking, but how well your decking performs will depend in large part on what it’s made out of. To help you plan your new roof, let’s look at some of your options!
Types of Roof Decking
In the vast majority of cases, roof decking is made of wood. There are exceptions, though, and several types of wood to choose from. If you’re getting a new roof installed, your roof decking material options include:

 	Plywood: Plywood is the most popular decking material in Florida, largely thanks to its relative affordability and strength. For decking, these boards usually come in 4x8 sheets. This means damaged sections can easily be replaced without removing larger sections of your decking.
 	Oriented Stand Board (OSB): This is one of the strongest roof decking material options on the market. To create these strong, resilient wooden boards, manufacturers press together wood strands and then use adhesives to reinforce their connections. The result is a sturdy material that will last for the life of your roof if it isn’t damaged.
 	Particleboard: A much more budget-friendly option, particleboard is made from compressed wood chips and industrial adhesives. This isn’t as strong as plywood or OSB, largely because it’s less moisture-resistant.
 	Metal Decking: The materials used in metal decking are usually steel, aluminum, or a combination of both. These metal sheets are hardy and offer unmatched strength, but they’re rarely chosen for decking because of their high costs. The exception to this is commercial structures that may need additional support.

There is no shortage of options when it comes to roof decking materials. And which one you choose will have long-lasting effects on your roof. But regardless of the type of decking you pick, damaged decking can lead to a lot of problems for your home. So how do you know when your decking has been damaged?
Signs of Damaged Decking
In general, it can be hard to tell when decking is damaged. That’s because it sits underneath the rest of your roof, so there’s no easy way to visually inspect your decking without removing a portion of your roof. Still, in some cases, you can spot signs of severe roof decking damage if you know what to look for.

Signs of damaged roof decking include:

 	Water stains on the ceiling or interior walls
 	Roof sagging
 	Mold or mildew in your attic
 	Roof leaks when it rains

If you see any of the above issues in your home, it’s important to act quickly. Damaged to your decking can spread without warning. And once it's there, the only way to fix it is to remove a portion of your roof and replace the damaged sections. The more time damage has to spread, the more you can expect to pay for new decking!
What to Know About Roof Decking Costs


If you’re getting a roof replacement, any quote you get will likely depend on the state of your roof decking. Even with a professional inspection, roofers can’t see how your decking is holding up without removing part of your roof. This means that any roof replacement cost estimate will likely be off since contractors can’t know if they’ll need to replace your decking until they’re working on your roof.

Thankfully, this doesn’t usually affect the total roofing costs by much — usually a couple of hundred dollars at most. If large sections of your decking need to be replaced, though, the total price of your roof replacement can be significantly higher than anticipated. Realistically, if you haven’t seen any of the signs of damaged decking in your home, you shouldn’t count on damaged decking increasing the cost of your roof replacement by much.

Because of their simple manufacturing, most types of roof decking keep costs low. This means that you can count on a roof replacement quote to give you an accurate, reliable figure!

### Reroofing for Florida Homeowners

Oftentimes, homeowners think their only options are between roof replacement and repairs. But reroofing (also known as roof restoration) presents a unique middle ground that can help homeowners get long-lasting protection without making the up front investment of a roof replacement.

PITCH Roofing is here to answer all of your questions about reroofing in Florida. As veteran Florida roofers, we’ve provided all kinds of roof replacements, repairs, and reroofing services to communities across Central Florida. Now, stick with us as we break down roof restoration and whether or not it’s right for your situation!
What Is Reroofing?


A classic roof replacement involves tearing off your old roof and installing a new one in its place. But what if you skipped that first step and put a new roof on top of your old one? This is essentially the idea behind reroofing: putting a new roof on top of your old one.

This approach has a lot of benefits. For one thing, reroofing is cheaper. Since nobody has to take off your old roof, you don’t need to pay for disposal, and your overall labor costs will go down since there’s less work to complete. But is reroofing safe?

Yes, reroofing can be just as safe and reliable as a roof replacement. Assuming that there is no damage to your roof decking, then it should have no problem supporting the weight of shingles or even metal roofing. And as long as your new roofing material is correctly installed, it should have no problem protecting your home from the Florida elements.

This covers the basics of what reroofing is and how it works. But is it right for your home?
Should You Choose Reroofing in Florida?
Reroofing is great for a lot of situations, but it’s not always the right call. Signs that your roof is a good candidate for roof restoration include:

 	Having a shingle roof and wanting either new shingles or a metal roof. Other types of roofs are not compatible with reroofing.
 	Not having any leaks. Leaking water can damage your decking, which then would not be able to support the weight of two roofs.
 	Only having one layer of roofing on your home. Most homes can support the weight of two roofs, but three would be structurally unsafe.
 	Having a sloped roof. Reroofing does not work well for flat roofs, which need to be replaced at the end of their lifespans.

If your roof meets these criteria, then reroofing could be perfect for your home. Up to now though, we’ve only covered the good sides of roof restoration. To help you make an informed decision, we have to look at the downsides of reroofing as well as the positives.
Cons of Roof Restoration
Reroofing is a great way to save money while getting the protection of a new roof. It isn’t perfect, though. So what are the downsides of reroofing that you should know about before committing?

First, let’s talk about cost savings. As we’ve established, reroofing is cheaper than roof replacement because you have lower labor costs from not disposing of the old roof. You can only reroof once, though, before you have to replace the roof entirely. So what happens the next time you need a new roof?

Well, you (or whoever owns the property at that time) will have to pay for both roofs to be removed and disposed of. So in a sense, roof restoration just kicks the can down the line — you still have to pay for your roof to be removed eventually. There are situations where this isn’t a problem, though. If you think you’ll have more money in 20 years or you don’t plan to be in the home by then, reroofing can make a lot of sense.

The other issue is the stability of your home. If your decking has been damaged, it may not support the weight of a second roof. At PITCH Roofing, we take your safety seriously, and we would never install a roof that we didn’t know would protect your home. However, there is no way to check your roof decking without tearing off your old roof.

Does that mean roofers have to work blind? Absolutely not. When you choose us for your reroofing job, we’ll chat with you to make sure that your roof hasn’t shown any signs of damaged roof decking. While this is not as reliable as seeing your decking for ourselves, it’s the best way that we can make sure your roof is ready for the additional weight.

We’ve covered the good and the bad of reroofing, but don’t worry if you still have questions. PITCH has been doing this for a long time, so we know the burning questions local homeowners have about reroofing! Now, let’s get to answering them.
FAQs About Reroofing in Florida


Q: How much does reroofing cost compared to a roof replacement?

A: Reroofing is less expensive than a full roof replacement because it involves lower labor and material costs. However, the exact cost will depend on the size of the roof, materials used, and which roofers you pick. To find out how much reroofing will cost you, the best thing you can do is start collecting roofing quotes.

Q: How long does reroofing last?

A: When getting a second layer of shingles installed, you can expect them to last for 15-20 years. The numbers are slightly different for metal roofs, which may last an additional 5-10 years but will not last as long as a newly installed metal roof on new decking.

Q: Does roof restoration come with warranties?

A: Yes, most roof restoration jobs come with both workmanship and material warranties. However, these warranties will likely not last as long as those for a roof replacement since your new roof will sit on top of someone else’s old work.

Q: How long does reroofing take?

A: Since nobody needs to remove your old roof, reroofing jobs are quick. They can usually be completed in just a day or two, although the size and dimensions of your roof will be a factor.

Q: Will reroofing add too much weight to my home?

A: If you only have one layer of shingles, reroofing typically won’t add too much weight. However, if the roof already has multiple layers or the structure is weak, the added weight could cause problems, and a roof replacement may be a safer option.

### Identifying Roof Hail Damage in Florida & How to Get Help

Florida is famous for its warmth and humidity, but we still get the occasional hailstorm. Unfortunately, local roofs aren’t immune to the impact damage that this can cause. That’s why it’s useful to be able to identify hail damage on your roof and have roofers you can rely on to fix the damage.

We’re PITCH Roofing, and as your local roofing partner, we consider it our job to make sure you’re ready for Florida’s unpredictable weather. If you think your roof may have sustained hail damage or you just want to get ready, keep reading our guide to identifying and fixing hail damage to your roof!
How to Identify Hail Damage on a Roof


Hailstorms can be surprisingly dangerous. Hail doesn’t have to be very large to pack a big punch, and while your roofing system is made to withstand some impact damage, no roof is totally immune to large chunks of ice falling on it.

The first step in seeing if your roof has hail damage is getting up on your roof to take a look. Make sure to wait until all inclement weather has passed, and never try to access your roof unless you’re 100% confident in your ability to do so safely. If you can’t access your roof for any reason, it’s best to schedule a roof inspection with licensed roofers who will be able to get on your roof and will know exactly what to look for.

If you do decide to inspect your roof yourself, then you’ll need to look carefully to see if your roof has been damaged. Some of the different signs of hail damage to your roof include:

 	Missing granules from your shingles, which can include finding granules in your gutters
 	Shiny appearance on your shingles
 	Random, widely spread roof indentations
 	Dents or bends in your roof’s flashing
 	Spots of discoloration on your roof, especially if they’re black

As you can see, hail damage to a roof can take many different forms. If you take a look at your roof and think that it may be damaged, then it’s important to get licensed roofers out there ASAP to resolve the issue.
Finding Hail Damage Roof Repair Contractors
When you have a damaged roof, time is everything. In its early stages, roof hail damage isn’t the biggest deal. It may be unsightly, but it’s not usually an immediate threat to the health of your roof. That changes over time, though.

With time, any damage to your roof can become exponentially worse. A small opening in your roof can become a waterway, and once water gets into your roofing system, you’re looking at much more extensive and expensive repairs.

That’s why we strongly encourage homeowners to seek out hail damage roof repair services. But the urgency of getting repairs doesn’t mean that you should entrust your roof to just anyone. FAQs About Roof Repairs After a Hailstorm
1. Q: What should I do if I think my roof was hit by hail?

A: Once the storm has passed, inspect your roof for hail damage. If you find signs of damage, you’ll want to call in a professional contractor to determine the exact type of damage and how severe it is so that you can work out a plan for comprehensive repairs.

2. Q: Does homeowners insurance cover hail damage to a roof?

A: In most cases, homeowners insurance plans cover acts of God, which would include hail damage to your roof. To verify your own coverage, we recommend checking your policy or speaking with your insurance representative.

3. Q: What happens if hail damage isn’t addressed quickly?

A: Untreated hail damage can lead to water leaks, mold growth, weakened roof structures, and reduced insulation effectiveness. Over time, this can result in higher repair costs and a shorter lifespan for your roof.

4. Q: How long does it take to repair hail damage on a roof?

A: The time required for repairs depends on the extent of the damage. Minor repairs might take a few hours, while more significant damage could take several days. Your contractor can provide a more accurate timeline after an inspection.

5. Q: Will hail damage lower my home’s resale value?

A: Untreated hail damage can make your home less appealing to buyers since it weakens your roof’s overall structure, which could in turn lower your home’s value. Thankfully, promptly addressing hail damage is a great way to prevent long-term damage and keep your home at its maximum value.

### How Much Does a New Shingle Roof Cost in Florida?

Shingles are the most popular roofing material both in Florida and across North America. But despite their popularity, many homeowners still have questions about this classic option. Whether you have questions about color options, composition, or shingle roof costs, we’ve got answers for you!

How Do Shingle Roofs Work?


Before we start our deep dive into shingle roof costs, it’s important to know what you’re paying for. Asphalt shingle roofs are made from fiberglass baseboards which are then coated in asphalt and topped with protective stone granules. Contractors will then arrange these shingles in overlapping patterns to create a strong, water-resistant barrier.

Nowadays, you might see the odd roof with 3-tab shingles, but architectural shingles have become the gold standard. These shingles are about twice as thick as 3-tab shingles, which gives them better wind and water resistance. At a glance, some of the best features of architectural asphalt shingles include:

 	Rated for winds up to 130 mph
 	Available in nearly any color you could imagine
 	Long-lasting material and workmanship warranties
 	Lifespan of 20-25 years
 	Low material and installation costs
 	Highly water-resistant when properly installed

These are the basics of what asphalt shingles are and how they work as a roofing system. But if you want to know how much a shingle roof costs in Florida, then there are a few factors to take into consideration.
How Much Does the Average Shingle Roof Cost in Florida?


Many homeowners want to know how much the average shingle roof costs to help plan their own roof replacement. If this sounds like you, then we can help — the average shingle roof costs in Florida are between $11,000 and $17,000.

While this number can be a helpful starting place, it isn’t everything. At the end of the day, your shingle roof replacement costs will be unique to your home and your shingles. And the only way to get a completely reliable figure is to receive a personalized roof replacement quote.

Material Costs
Unsurprisingly, the price of your shingles will have a profound impact on your total roof replacement costs. Thankfully, architectural shingles are available at very affordable rates. On average, asphalt architectural shingles cost between $4 and $9 per square foot.

While this is by no means cheap, it does make shingles one of the most affordable roofing materials on the market. National roofing companies, on the other hand, often have to charge more to offset the costs of their larger staff and operating costs.
Size and Pitch of Your Roof
With the cost of asphalt shingles being by the square foot, it makes sense that a larger roof would come with higher roof replacement costs. After all, the bigger the roof, the more shingles your roofers have to buy, and the longer contractors will take to install them. But this isn’t the only roofing factor that influences how much a shingle roof costs.

The pitch of your roof will also heavily impact price. Most residential roofs have a pitch between 4:12 and 9:12. Roofs with lower pitches may not be suitable for shingles, but roofs with a steeper pitch can cost more to replace. That’s because working on these roofs requires specialized safety equipment so that your contractors can safely work on your roof without the risk of falling. This increases both material costs as well as roofing labor costs.
Accessibility
When getting a new roof, it helps to make it easy for your roofers to get on and off your roof. With a shingle roof replacement, roofers have to be able to remove your old roof, dispose of it, and install your new shingles. In other words, they need space to temporarily place a dumpster on your property and access your roof without much difficulty.

For these reasons, cars in the driveway and thick shrubs around the home can increase how much your shingle roof costs. If roofers have to take extra time to carefully navigate your property, their labor costs can quickly pile up. That’s why we recommend clearing your yard as much as possible before your scheduled shingle roof replacement!

### New Construction Roofing vs. Roof Replacement: Understanding the Key Differences

Whether you're building a new home or upgrading an existing one, the roof is one of the most critical components. It not only protects your home but also affects its energy efficiency, curb appeal, and resale value. But what's the difference between new construction roofing and a roof replacement, and why does it matter?
What Is New Construction Roofing?


New construction roofing involves the complete installation of a roof on a brand-new building. Unlike a roof replacement, there’s no old roof to remove, which often makes the process simpler in some ways but requires more intensive planning to ensure the new roof is structurally sound.

Key Steps in New Construction Roofing Include:

 	Roof Design and Material Selection: Since there is no existing roof, the choice of materials is flexible. Common options include asphalt shingles, metal, tile, and flat roofing solutions.
 	Installing the Roof Deck: This involves laying the initial layer of sheathing over the rafters, which provides the foundation for the roofing material.
 	Adding Underlayment and Flashing: A water-resistant barrier and flashing are essential to protect against leaks.
 	Attaching the Roofing Material: Depending on the chosen material, shingles, tiles, or metal sheets are added.

With new construction, homeowners can prioritize customization, ensuring that both the roof design and material meet their style and functionality needs.
What Is Roof Replacement?
A roof replacement involves removing an existing roof and replacing it with a new one. Roof replacement is common when the current roof shows signs of age, leaks, or damage that can't be repaired. While the end goal is the same—installing a reliable roof—the process is more complex due to the additional step of removing the old materials.

Steps in Roof Replacement Include:

 	Old Roof Removal: The existing roof material, underlayment, and any damaged components are removed. This is often labor-intensive and requires careful disposal of materials.
 	Inspection of Roof Decking: After removal, contractors inspect the roof decking to ensure it's structurally sound. If the decking is damaged, it will need to be repaired or replaced.
 	Installation of New Underlayment and Roofing Material: Once the old roof is cleared, new underlayment, flashing, and roofing materials are installed, similar to the new construction process.

Price Differences: New Construction Roofing vs. Roof Replacement
1. Material Costs
The materials used for new construction and replacement roofs are generally the same, but replacements may involve additional costs if damaged decking or structural components need repair.

 	Asphalt Shingles: Typically $3.50–$5.50 per square foot.
 	Metal Roofing: Around $7.00–$20.00 per square foot.
 	Tile Roofing: Between $6.00–$18.00 per square foot.

2. Labor Costs
Labor for new construction roofing can be less expensive because the process is straightforward, with no demolition required. Roof replacements, however, often incur higher labor costs due to the additional steps involved in removing the old roof and disposing of materials.

On average, labor costs are as follows:

 	New Construction Roofing: $1.50–$3.00 per square foot
 	Roof Replacement: $2.50–$4.00 per square foot

3. Additional Costs

 	Demolition and Disposal: Roof replacements require the removal of old materials, which can add $1,000–$2,000 to the overall cost, depending on the roof size and material.
 	Permit Fees and Inspections: Some municipalities require different permits for replacements, especially if structural repairs are needed.

Structural Considerations: The Framework Differences


One key difference between new construction roofing and roof replacement lies in the structural support. With new construction, the roof’s framework and decking are designed to support the weight of the chosen roofing material, allowing homeowners to opt for heavier options like tile. In roof replacements, it’s crucial to verify that the existing framework can support the new material. For example, switching from asphalt shingles to a heavier tile roof may require reinforcing the decking or rafters, adding to the project cost.
Timing: Project Timelines and Planning
New Construction Roofing: Since new construction roofing is part of the overall build, it is usually easier to plan and schedule. Contractors can work according to the general construction timeline, without needing to account for existing roof demolition.

Roof Replacement: Roof replacements depend on the condition of the existing roof. Replacements may require waiting periods for insurance assessments, particularly if storm damage is involved. Additionally, unexpected weather changes can delay roof replacement projects, as existing roofs left exposed must be protected from water and debris.
Benefits and Considerations for Each Option
New Construction Roofing Benefits:

 	Complete design flexibility allows you to choose from a wider range of materials.
 	Easier installation without demolition, which can reduce labor costs and timeline.

Roof Replacement Benefits:

 	Ideal for upgrading an older roof to a more durable or energy-efficient material.
 	Allows for thorough inspection and necessary repairs, ensuring long-term structural integrity.

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)
Q: How much does a new construction roof cost compared to a replacement?
A: New construction roofs are often less expensive due to the lack of demolition costs. However, costs vary based on materials, roof size, and labor. Roof replacements may include additional expenses for removal and disposal of old materials.

Q: Is there a difference in the lifespan of a new construction roof vs. a replacement roof?
A: Both can have similar lifespans if quality materials and installation practices are used. The lifespan generally depends more on the material used (e.g., asphalt shingles typically last 20-30 years, while metal or tile roofs can last 50 years or more).

Q: Can I change the roofing material for a replacement roof?
A: Yes, you can change materials during a replacement. However, some materials, like tile, are heavier and may require reinforcement of the existing framework.

Q: What are the most durable roofing materials for new construction?
A: Metal and tile roofs are known for their durability and longevity. Asphalt shingles are affordable and widely used but may have a shorter lifespan in comparison.

Q: Do new construction roofs come with warranties?
A: Yes, new construction roofs typically come with warranties on materials and installation, especially when installed by certified contractors. Replacements often include warranties as well, which vary based on materials and installer.

### Next Steps for Your Insurance Roof Replacement: A Complete Guide After Approval

After a storm or another unexpected event damages your roof, filing a homeowners' insurance claim can feel overwhelming. Once you receive approval from your insurance company, you’ve tackled one of the biggest hurdles. But what comes next? This guide will walk you through each of the following steps to ensure that your insurance roof replacement goes smoothly and results in a durable, high-quality roof.
Confirm the Scope of Your Insurance Coverage
Before moving forward with your roof replacement, verify the details of what your insurance company has approved. Some important areas to confirm include:

 	Material Coverage: Check if the approved claim covers the roofing material you prefer. For instance, if you are considering switching from asphalt shingles to a more durable material like metal or tile, ensure that your insurance approval aligns with this choice.
 	Labor and Disposal Costs: These can vary depending on the policy. Make sure that your coverage includes the labor for removing and replacing your roof, as well as the disposal of old materials.
 	Upgrades for Local Code Compliance: Some regions in Florida require certain roofing standards or materials to meet building codes, particularly regarding storm resilience. If your insurance policy includes coverage for code-required upgrades, verify whether these improvements are covered by your claim.

Knowing what’s covered ensures that both you and your contractor are on the same page, helping avoid unexpected expenses or miscommunications down the line.


Find a Trusted Roofing Contractor
Choosing a reliable roofing contractor is essential for ensuring a high-quality replacement. Look for a contractor with experience in insurance roof replacements and a reputation for integrity and professionalism. Consider the following when making your choice:

 	Insurance Expertise: A roofing company experienced in insurance claims can simplify the process by guiding you through any additional documentation or required steps. They’ll understand the nuances of working with insurers, which can help avoid unnecessary delays.
 	Certifications and Reviews: Select a contractor who is BBB Accredited, highly rated on platforms like GuildQuality, and certified, such as an Owens Corning Preferred Contractor. These qualifications signal quality workmanship and adherence to industry standards.
 	Licensed Adjuster on Staff: Some roofing companies, like PITCH Roofing, have a licensed insurance adjuster on staff who can help interpret the approval details and communicate with your insurance company to keep the process efficient and hassle-free.

Once you’ve selected a reputable roofing company, schedule a time for an initial inspection to confirm the damage, materials, and scope of work.
Schedule an Initial Inspection and Document All Existing Damage
The next step involves having your chosen contractor perform an in-depth inspection of your roof. This inspection is essential for determining the full extent of damage and confirming any details that may impact the insurance payout or coverage.

 	Take Photos and Videos: Documenting the damage with photos and videos protects you and provides further evidence of the roof’s condition. Having these on file can help in case any discrepancies arise between your initial claim and the work being performed.
 	Discuss Material Recommendations: Based on the approved claim, discuss the materials recommended by your contractor. Options like asphalt shingles, metal, and tile each come with unique advantages that can affect durability, cost, and aesthetics. If upgrading materials, double-check that the insurance approval will accommodate any changes.

Pro Tip: Request a written, itemized estimate from your contractor after the inspection. This ensures transparency and provides a reference in case of any questions or follow-up from your insurer.
Plan for the Project Timeline
With your insurance approval, contractor selection, and inspection complete, it’s time to plan the actual project timeline. Understanding each step of the replacement process will help you prepare for disruptions and ensure that all work is done correctly.

 	Schedule the Project: Work with your contractor to schedule the project, keeping in mind the weather forecast. In Florida, planning around the rainy season is essential, as weather delays can impact timelines.
 	Removal and Installation: The first day of work typically involves removing the old roof. Once the roof is cleared, the new roofing materials will be installed according to code, followed by final touches like sealing and inspections.

Manage Payments and Organize Necessary Documents
Once work begins, it’s important to manage payments and documents required by your insurance company. Some insurers may require you to submit invoices or proof of work at various stages, so staying organized will streamline the reimbursement or payment process.

Common Documents to Track Include:

 	Invoices and Receipts: Keep records of all invoices and receipts related to labor, materials, and disposal. This documentation will be essential if your insurer requests evidence of work or costs.
 	Adjuster Sign-Offs: Some insurance companies may require the adjuster to sign off on each stage of the work before disbursing additional funds. Make sure your contractor is aware of this requirement if it applies.
 	Lien Waivers: After making the final payment, obtain a lien waiver from your contractor. This waiver protects you from any future claims on your property related to unpaid bills.

Organizing these documents in a digital or physical folder will make it easy to reference them throughout the project.

After the roof replacement is complete, it’s time for a final inspection. The purpose of this inspection is to confirm that the work was completed to your standards and complies with local codes and insurance requirements. During this stage, you should:

 	Review Warranty Information: Confirm the details of your roof warranty, ideally one that covers both materials and labor. Warranties from trusted manufacturers like Owens Corning offer additional peace of mind.
 	Plan for Ongoing Maintenance: Regular maintenance is crucial for extending the life of your roof. Many roofing companies, including PITCH Roofing, offer annual maintenance plans to help keep your roof in top condition, which may also help keep insurance premiums stable.

### Types of Tile Roofs for Your Next Roof Replacement

Tile roofing has a deep, rich history in Florida. While the core components of tile roofing have remained the same across the centuries, modern tile roofing comes with more options than ever. This gives homeowners almost unlimited customization options, but it can also be overwhelming if you’re not familiar with all the types of tile roofs.

That’s what we’re here for. We’re PITCH Roofing, and as your trusted local roofers, it’s our job to answer all your questions about roofing options in Florida. Stick with us as we walk you through all the types of tile roofs available to you in the Sunshine State!
Types of Tile Roofs in Florida


When it comes to the types of tile roof materials, there are really only two options: concrete and clay. While each of these options can give you a high-quality tile roof, there are a lot of differences both in their performance and cost. To help you plan the best tile roof replacement for your home, let’s take an in-depth look at these materials!
Concrete Tiles
If you’re looking for an affordable kind of tile roof, concrete tiles are perfect. In general, concrete roofing tiles cost about $15 per square foot. This is still much more expensive than asphalt shingles, of course, but you’re also paying for quality.

Concrete tiles have great wind resistance, with most types of concrete tiles being able to withstand winds up to 150 mph. They’re also Class A fire resistant and stand up well against water damage, which makes them hardy and durable protection for your home.

These roofing tiles also last much longer than asphalt shingles. On average, a concrete tile roof will last for about 50 years in Florida — twice as long as an asphalt shingle roof! And unlike a shingle roof, concrete tiles don’t need much in the way of maintenance and repairs.

If there is one downside, it’s the color of concrete tiles. While these tiles last a long time, their color doesn’t hold up as well. Over time, the color lightens as the sun bleaches the tile. In these circumstances, homeowners can invest in re-painting services to restore the tiles’ original color.
Clay Tiles
Clay roofing tiles are a high-end roofing material, which comes with both a high cost and outstanding performance. For this type of tile roof, you can expect to pay around $20 per square foot. That is a premium cost, but what kind of product are you getting for that investment?]

Well, clay tile roofs have all the great protective features of concrete tiles and then some. That means 150 mph wind resistance, Class A fire resistance, and great water resistance. They also aren’t painted, unlike concrete tiles, which means the sun won’t bleach them.

These are all great features of clay tile roofs, but none of them are the main selling point. The biggest reason that homeowners pick clay tiles is for their unmatched longevity. Clay tile roofs last the longest of any roofing material, with some clay tile roofs staying in place for a century or more with proper maintenance and repairs. There may not be such a thing as a “forever roof,” but clay tiles are certainly close!

To top it all off, clay roofing tiles come in a variety of colors. Whether you like the classic clay red, neutral earth tones, or something zanier, you can bet that your perfect tile roof is out there.
Styles of Tile Roofs in Florida


We’ve covered the different types of tile roofing materials, but there are also many options when it comes to the cut and style of your roofing tiles. To help you pick the best option for your new roof, let’s look at these different types of tile roofs one by one!

 	S-Shaped (Spanish) Tiles: These tiles are famous for their shape, which helps with water shedding and makes them perfect for Florida’s rainy season. They also have a distinctly Florida aesthetic and have been in the Sunshine State since the earliest Spanish colonialists arrived.
 	Barrel (Mission) Tiles: Barrel tiles have a distinctive cylindrical shape, like a barrel cut in half. This improves ventilation on your roof and helps keep everything cooler, which in turn can lower your monthly energy bill.
 	French Tiles: French tiles have two flutes that run down the center of the tile, making water drainage easy. With their textured appearance, these tiles are great for adding personality and visual interest to your roof.
 	Flat Tiles: Like the name implies, these tiles are flat, which makes them look more like shingles than other types of tile roofs. These create a sleek, modern look that is very popular for contemporary-style homes in Florida.
 	Pantile Tiles: With a highly curved profile, pantile tiles create a wave-like pattern similar to S-shaped tiles but with more pronounced curves. This creates a dynamic pattern across your roof that is a popular combination with European architecture.

As you can see, there are more than a few options when it comes to tile roofing. But whatever type of tile roof you prefer, the first step in getting your new roof is always collecting estimates.
